So I used to wish I was born on the 10th or the 12th. I actually didn’t celebrate my birthday from ages 10 to 13. It just felt inappropriate and weird to be so happy when everyone else was not. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve told people my birthday, and it becomes a whole conversation. When I need ID at a bar or when I have to pick up a prescription, and they ask me for my birthday, they’re like, “Really?” I’ve even had people ask me, “What was that like for you?” And I have to say, “Well, I was not even born yet so I was not aware of anything.” I’ve learned to just say my birthday is in September. However, as I’ve gotten older, I’ve realized that I like my birthday. It’s such a beautiful time of year. I’m at the point where I can acknowledge that it was sad, but I can also celebrate myself. All my friends tell me that when they think of 9/11, they think of me as their first thought. 
Keira: When something tragic happens, it’s a beautiful thing to be around a newborn baby. My brother’s wife lost her first husband on the 10th, and his funeral was on the 13th. She adores Freya because, in her world, she’s a bright light at a dark moment. We have a lot of friends who say that year after year: She was the shining light that day. –As told to B.L.

articles.title: NATO has no plans to deploy nuclear weapons to additional countries — Polish official
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 3. /TASS/. NATO is not considering the deployment of nuclear warheads to additional countries as part of its Nuclear Sharing program, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said.
"As of today, the deployment of nuclear warheads beyond the places already hosting them is not on the [NATO] agenda," he told RMF FM.
However, the Polish defense official clarified that Warsaw sought to participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence concept and that it was one of the issues on the agenda. "For the first time, we have been able to make sure that NATO countries are willing to include Poland in the nuclear sharing program, which is a very serious one," Zalewski noted.
On August 27, Zalewski said at a press conference at the NATO headquarters in Brussels that Poland had neither the desire nor plans to host nuclear weapons. He explained that Warsaw would like to be part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence strategy without having nuclear arms stationed in the country.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki said in an interview with Polsat television in mid-February that Warsaw should seek access to nuclear weapons. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, in turn, stressed that the authorities were not considering such an option. However, Prime Minister Donald Tusk spoke of the country’s interest in the "nuclear umbrella" project proposed by French President Emmanuel Macron.

articles.title: Lebanon disarmament plan stalls as Hezbollah shifts to guerrilla tactics
articles.body:
It is now clear that something is not working in the mechanism that was supposed to bring calm to the northern border. The pilot program in southern Lebanon, designed to pave the way for Hezbollah’s disarmament south of the Litani River, an IDF withdrawal and the transfer of responsibility to the Lebanese army, is not progressing as expected.
Israel’s defense establishment has identified significant difficulties facing the Lebanese army, which is not operating in accordance with the targets set for it. Because of a legal limitation, its soldiers avoid searches inside homes and terror infrastructure in villages, preferring to focus only on open and public areas.
Beyond the difficulties on the ground, the root of the problem lies at the diplomatic level. So far, no agreement has been reached on who will supervise the Lebanese army’s work, what criteria it will be required to meet and what exact conditions the IDF will need to approve before beginning a withdrawal.
About two months ago, ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth reported on a proposal under which Italian military forces would supervise the process, but that plan has yet to get off the ground.
The deadlock has two sides. On the one hand, it gives the IDF vital room to complete its mission on the Ali Taher ridge, where dozens of Hezbollah terrorists are currently trapped. It also allows the forces to improve their holding model, establish better command infrastructure and continue clearing the area and denying Hezbollah the infrastructure it developed over the years.
On the other hand, a prolonged stay in southern Lebanon raises familiar concerns, foremost among them a return to the difficult and bloody days of the past.
Meanwhile, the fighting on the Ali Taher ridge is progressing well and creating considerable tension within Hezbollah. That was evident overnight, when the terror organization launched two explosive drones toward forces operating in the area. The incident ended without casualties after one drone was intercepted and the other fell.
A study published by the Alma Research and Education Center, which researches security challenges in northern Israel, points to a significant change in Hezbollah’s operational pattern as the organization adapts to the new reality.
After the threat of an invasion of the Galilee suffered a severe blow and Radwan Force infrastructure was destroyed, the organization abandoned broad operational plans and shifted to decentralized guerrilla activity by small cells, in a format similar to that now familiar from the Gaza Strip.
Security officials say Hezbollah continues to gather intelligence on IDF troops, study how they operate, map locations and identify methods of operation in preparation for a scenario in which fighting resumes in the form of infiltrations, ambushes, explosive-drone launches and the laying of explosive devices.
To pull the pilot program out of the deadlock, Israel is trying to apply American pressure on the Lebanese government and army, based on the assessment that completion of the IDF’s operation on the Ali Taher ridge, together with diplomatic contacts mediated by the United States, will force the sides to move forward, formulate an agreed enforcement force and set clear criteria.
Northern Command is preparing the area for the holiday period and the onset of winter. The preparations include driving drills, opening routes and combat training for extreme weather conditions.
At the tactical level, the main focus is on dealing with the threat posed by explosive drones.
“We will come to the next round better prepared when it comes to the drone threat,” a security official told ynet.
In the absence of a broad technological solution, troops are being trained in protective procedures, the deployment of defensive nets and interception methods, alongside several new systems that have already become operational in the field.
It is important to note that the work carried out by the IDF in the current maneuver, which began with Operation Roaring Lion, has been highly significant and has struck nearly all of Hezbollah’s systems.
Ultimately, the situation on the northern border remains a direct result of the balance with Iran.
Israel’s defense establishment assesses that if the situation between Washington and Tehran escalates further and Israel is drawn into it, that will have an immediate impact on the Lebanese arena as well.
The Middle East pressure cooker is once again approaching boiling point just as the already tense holiday period begins, with the confrontation between the United States and Iran escalating again and putting Israel’s defense establishment on the highest level of alert.
All this is taking place against the backdrop of an escalation across the various arenas, from aggressive activity in Gaza and the West Bank to increased pressure in Lebanon. At the same time, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been holding tense talks with the U.S. ambassadors to Israel and Lebanon over the southern Lebanon pilot plan, which, as noted, is not progressing as expected.

articles.title: Berlin’s latest Russia panic is reckless even by its own standards
articles.body:
Berlin’s latest Russia panic is reckless even by its own standards
When you’ve burned all your bridges, go and burn some more.
That seems to be the unspoken strategy of Berlin’s policy toward Moscow, which is the only plausible interpretation of Germany’s fresh efforts to damage its already abysmal relationship with Russia. Not that they have come as a surprise. Since the odd drone incident at the Leipzig/Halle airport at the beginning of August, the German political establishment and its always compliant mainstream media have been preparing the ground for explicitly blaming Moscow.
The German public has been subject to what looks like a systematic campaign of escalating innuendo for almost a month. The story emerging from this barrage of unfounded claims and speculation masquerading as self-evident certainty has been changing: the role of an airport bus driver merely discovering the drone sitting quietly on the tarmac next to an extra-large Ukrainian transport plane or kicking it to the ground with a Bruce-Lee-type flying kick, as initially claimed, has remained unclear and contradictory. Initial reports of another drone colliding with a plane in flight had to be retracted when traces of birds became too obvious.
Now, clearly, the time has come to make things official. The German government, represented by Minister of the Interior Alexander Dobrindt and foreign policy chief Johann Wadephul, has blamed the drone incident on Russian intelligence services and announced retaliation measures, such as closing a consulate and cultural center in Berlin, even more travel restrictions and individual sanctions on Russians, and fresh attempts to go after Russian ships by, in effect, piracy. The Russian ambassador has been called in, various EU governments, the EU commission, and NATO – though not the US – have made a grand show out of supporting Germany.
Moscow has roundly rejected Berlin’s accusations, called in the German chargé d’affaires, and promised a symmetric response to Germany’s actions. President Vladimir Putin has plausibly described them as a “grave mistake” and, equally plausibly, surmised that it is due mainly to attempts to shape elections and distract from Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s historically sensational unpopularity.
So far, so bad: Berlin has managed to reach a new low-point in a relationship that is crucial for Germany but which it loves to tear apart. As Sarah Wagenknecht of the new-left BSW party has noted, the drone did not do any damage, regardless of the question of where it came from. The German government, though, has deliberately chosen a massive over-reaction. The new-right AfD’s Ulrich Siegmund, likely to soon make history by winning the AfD’s first state elections, has also called for moderation and dialogue instead of escalation. In today’s Germany, reason is literally on the political margins, while the self-declared Center has gone nuts.
What is even worse, however, is that no proof has been presented of Russian involvement. It is true that after the announcement of Berlin’s official blame game, conveniently timed leaks to the mainstream media have conveyed unsubstantiated claims about two holders of Russian passports being involved. But this conspicuous combination of a specific accusation presented without evidence and clearly coordinated leaks merely hinting at it makes the impression of manipulation even worse.
Not to speak of the fact that these passports – if they exist and if they actually belong to real perpetrators – are extremely flimsy and, frankly, bizarre pieces of evidence: Why would Russian intelligence services make sure their agents carry Russian passports? If anyone had an interest in making it that easy to point fingers at Moscow it would surely be either Ukraine, which has a vile record in terrorist false flag operations, lying, and subterfuge of the worst sort. For Kiev, it would have been ideal to place a drone that creates hysteria in Berlin but fails to destroy an asset as valuable and rare as the AN-124 Condor transport aircraft.
The fact that the West in general and Germany in particular already has a long record of proven false alarms about Russian drones has also made no difference. As the Germans say, where there’s a will, there’s a way. And the will to deepen tensions with Russia is boundless among the current German establishment.
Speaking of which, it is impossible not to be stunned by the difference between Berlin’s treatment of a devastating terror attack which did actually work and one that either failed or was staged to begin with: We now know that Ukraine – most likely with the help of one or more NATO states – committed the 2022 Nord Stream pipeline attack, that is the single worst sabotage of postwar Germany’s vital infrastructure, economy, and environment while blaming Russia.
Yet Berlin has shown a consistent pattern of tolerating or even helping with the cover-up, while going as slow as possible on investigation and prosecution, while Ukraine’s leader Vladimir Zelensky keeps boldly lying. That is the state of the art almost four years after the attack. That and a relentless and unceasing flow of gazillions of German taxpayers’ money to the Kiev perpetrator regime. So much for “not rewarding the aggressor”: National masochism is too kind a term.
After the Leipzig/Halle incident it has taken less than a month to come to sweeping conclusions and reach for strong retaliatory measures while not presenting evidence. What a contrast. Clearly, those commentators are right who guess that Berlin’s newfound capacity for rapid over-reaction is rooted in several aggressive policy agendas: the current push to turn the German foreign intelligence service BND into an instrument of sabotage paramilitary operations; the new militarism which aims to build the most powerful conventional army in Europe and is explicitly targeting Moscow, and, last but not least, turning hatred and fear of Russia into a distraction in a country in deep economic crisis.
If Berlin is not preparing for open war with Russia, it is certainly doing its best to leave precisely that impression. Many Germans do not agree with this road-to-perdition course. For all of Europe’s sake, let’s hope that they will finally manage to change it.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: Trump aides seek 'quiet' in Iran war before November elections
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump aides seek 'quiet' in Iran war but say attacks may intensify after November elections
Top aides to President Donald Trump are pushing to keep the Iran war from escalating before November's midterm elections to staunch Republican electoral losses, four people familiar with the discussions said, a strategy already under strain as the US and Iran exchanged back-and-forth attacks overnight.
White House officials will consider ramping up military action after the 3 November vote, said the sources, who requested anonymity to describe internal thinking, though any return to full-scale conflict is far from a given. The US military said its latest strikes were retaliation for recent attacks on American forces and marine traffic in the region.
For now, the sources said, the administration wants to rely on applying more economic pressure on Iran in an effort to extract concessions in any future negotiation that months of military action failed to secure.
"We are keeping the pressure on Iran," one White House official said. "But November is a priority."
Keeping the war mostly contained until then would help prevent the unpopular conflict from dominating the news as Trump's Republicans campaign to defend thin majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, said the sources, three of whom are White House officials.
Only 31% of Americans approve of the war, while some 63% disapprove, according to a late August Reuters/Ipsos poll, and voters are particularly unhappy about high gas prices.
A tactical pause could also give the US military some breathing room to replenish its heavily depleted munitions stockpiles, the sources said.
But pulling off the play-it-cool strategy looks more difficult by the day. While the conflict remains much less intense than it was during the spring or during a flare-up in the middle of the summer, both sides have exchanged tit-for-tat strikes in recent days.
Iran's leaders, emboldened after months of disrupting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and facing little internal unrest, will likely keep striking at US and allied Gulf targets, including military bases, vessels and energy infrastructure, at least periodically, analysts said.
The US will face pressure to retaliate, potentially leading to an escalatory spiral that brings both sides back to a full-scale air war—whether the administration wants it or not.
Over the weekend, the US struck rocket launchers on Iran's Larak Island, prompting Iran to fire missiles toward Jordan and the United Arab Emirates. The US hit more Iranian targets around the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday in the biggest outbreak of fighting since July, a fresh outburst of violence that killed military personnel and civilians in Iran.
"The regime has every incentive to disrupt the 'calm'—which is no real calm, after all, since the administration's explicit aim is to increase economic pressure massively on Iran," said Barbara Leaf, who served as the top State Department official for the Middle East under former President Joe Biden.
Another wild card is Trump himself.
The president's approval rating has fallen from 40% to 33% since the conflict began, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling. Sources said he is not currently interested in escalation, but he is famously prone to changing his mind and could change course in response to events.
Trump threatened on Tuesday to escalate the conflict if Iran hits back against the latest US strikes.
"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings," he wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Trump on Wednesday said he did not think the renewed military campaign would last long. He also reiterated his position that the upcoming elections were not factoring into his Iran strategy.
"Number one, I'm not running. My party is running, and I'm going to help my party," he told reporters in the Oval Office. "But I think my party respects the fact that we're not allowing Iran to have a nuclear weapon."
Constrained by logistics and politics
As the US-Israeli war on Iran enters its seventh month, his White House finds itself increasingly constrained by logistical and political realities, however.
"The timetable has changed," one senior White House official said. Another added that the "calendar is driving Iran."
Reuters reported in August that the military had used "virtually all" of its supply of certain precision missiles. The Washington Post reported on Sunday that the heads of the Army, Navy and Air Force warned Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth in a written assessment that prolonging the war was unsustainable and would diminish the military's readiness in other theaters.
The Pentagon has said the military had "everything it needs to execute" its mission.
“President Trump has destroyed Iran’s military capabilities and is crippling what’s left of its abysmal economy with the most powerful naval blockade in world history and crushing sanctions," White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said. "The President will continue to advance America’s interests at home and abroad and will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon."
America's Gulf allies—some of whom had pushed for aggressive action against Iran earlier in the war to weaken their main regional adversary—roundly urged the White House to de-escalate after a recent round of attacks in late July, regional diplomats said.
Currently, two White House officials said, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are among the high-ranking Trump aides who are on board with the idea of trying to keep the Iran conflict relatively "quiet" until November.
In recent weeks, administration officials have instead intensified an economic isolation campaign, during which the US has threatened to slap countries that trade with Iran with massive sanctions, while maintaining its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.
The trade-focused strategy, however, has its own limits, analysts and officials said.
Iran has spent decades under layers of US and international sanctions that have battered its economy but have not deterred its leadership.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that the pressure campaign may cause Iran to lash out militarily, raising the prospect that the economic campaign could itself stoke military escalation.
Additionally, some major world powers, like China, have not joined Washington's bid to isolate Iran, prompting questions about the campaign's effectiveness.
"The purpose of the new sanctions package is meant to add economic pressure on top of that being caused by the blockade to force Iran back to the table, after the administration determined it was a better option than returning to kinetic action," said Alex Plitsas, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council. "Iran is concerned about it, but China has already indicated that it's not willing to play ball, which calls into question how effective it will be."

articles.title: Berlin approves $930 million in weapons sales to Israel
articles.body:
Berlin approves $930 million in weapons sales to Israel
The German government approved nearly €800 million ($930 million) in weapons exports to Israel between January and June, Der Spiegel reports, citing a government response to a parliamentary inquiry. The sum is already four times higher than the total value Berlin greenlighted last year.
Around one-fifth of the exports was linked to German-Israeli defense-industry cooperation benefiting the German Armed Forces, according to the government. Just over two-thirds of the approved value is tied to the INS Drakon, a nearly 70-meter-long Dolphin II-class submarine built for Israel by German shipbuilder TKMS. The vessel, which can remain submerged for weeks, left Kiel on Tuesday and is reportedly on its way to Israel.
Berlin said the remainder covered equipment not classified as ‘weapons of war’, including small arms, ammunition, explosives, and drones, according to Der Spiegel.
The Left Party accused Berlin of “boundless double standards” over the deals.
“As [Chancellor] Friedrich Merz was supposedly outraged by [Israeli Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir’s inhumane statements, his federal government was pushing ahead with cooperation with a government and an army facing genocide charges before the International Criminal Court, supporting settler violence in the West Bank, and continuing to occupy southern Lebanon,” MP Lea Reisner said.
The controversial Israeli minister stated last month that he considers the enclave “to be ours” and urged the IDF to carry out dozens of “targeted assassinations” there every night, claiming that some in the Palestinian enclave “are not people.”
Germany’s War Weapons Control Act requires licenses to “always be denied” where weapons risk being used in “peace-disturbing acts” or where Germany’s obligations under international law could be impaired.
Berlin temporarily halted weapons exports to Israel in August 2025 over West Jerusalem’s plans to occupy Gaza City, but lifted the restrictions in November after a US-backed ceasefire with Hamas. Israeli forces have since continued operations in Gaza and against Hezbollah in Lebanon, where they still occupy parts of the south.
Germany is meanwhile expanding military cooperation with Israel. On Wednesday, the German Navy said it had successfully tested an Israeli ballistic missile in the North Atlantic with a range of up to 500 kilometers. Germany has no ballistic missiles of its own, with Taurus cruise missiles being its longest-range missile systems.
Germany’s unwavering support for Israel, which is facing genocide accusations before the International Court of Justice in a case filed by South Africa, has arguably cost Berlin international support, as it failed to secure a seat on the Security Council in June.

articles.title: Pentagon limits classified access amid Iran war concerns - report
articles.body:
The Pentagon has restricted access to decades of classified military documents on an internal computer system, The Washington Post reported on Wednesday, days after the newspaper reported that senior US commanders had raised concerns about sustaining large-scale military operations against Iran.
Documents associated with the Secretary of Defense Orders Book (SDOB) were removed from an internal web portal on the Secret Internet Protocol Router Network (SIPRNet), according to three people familiar with the matter who spoke to The Washington Post on condition of anonymity.
It was not immediately clear whether the documents remained available to US personnel through other means or how the reduction in access could affect military planning, according to the report.
SIPRNet contains information classified as "secret," while top-secret information is held on more highly classified networks with fewer people granted access.
US military leaders raised concerns over Iran operations
The SDOB contains information on the location and availability of US warships, military units, weapons systems, and other resources. It also allows senior military leaders to formally register reservations about orders while continuing to carry them out through a process known as "non-concurring," The Washington Post reported.
The Jerusalem Post previously reported, citing the Washington Post, that several senior US military leaders raised concerns in the classified August 14 edition of the SDOB about continuing operations against Iran.
The officials warned that prolonging the war could weaken the US military's ability to respond to threats elsewhere. The SDOB reportedly called for some US troops deployed in the Middle East to remain in the region through September, while others would remain until 2027.
Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, head of US European Command; Gen. Francis Donovan, head of US Southern Command; Adm. Samuel Paparo, head of US Pacific Command; and Adm. Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, were among those who registered reservations with a "non-concur," according to people familiar with the discussion who spoke to the Washington Post.
Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach and acting Army Chief of Staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve agreed with Hegseth's plan to extend some unit deployments but emphasized that doing so would carry significant risks, according to the report.
Pentagon declines to discuss access change
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell declined to discuss the reported change with the Washington Post on Wednesday but did not dispute that it had occurred.
"As we have previously stated, the Department of War does not publicly discuss internal operational deliberative processes, including the management, handling, or access protocols for the Secretary of War Orders Book (SWOB)," Parnell said in a statement to the newspaper.
"The success of our service members is Secretary Hegseth's top priority, and for that reason, decisions regarding operational processes, force posture, and deliberative staffing are managed through appropriate security channels to ensure mission security and operational integrity," he added.
Following the Washington Post's Sunday report, Parnell said on social media that much of what the newspaper published was "inaccurate," though he did not specify which details he disputed.
"Non-concurs are standard," Parnell said. "The Secretary sees them constantly. That's how you run a real military. We are in great shape around the world."
Restricted access could complicate military planning
A former defense official who routinely reviewed the documents told the Washington Post that removing the SDOB from SIPRNet or moving it to systems with higher levels of classification would "dramatically reduce the number of people who have direct access to it."
Commanders and their staff rely on access to the SDOB for time-sensitive decisions and notifications, the former official told the newspaper.
Moving aircraft and weapons from one command to another, for example, requires urgent logistical work to redirect equipment and resources. Restricting access to the relevant information could make that process slower and more difficult, according to the former official.
The change does not make it impossible for personnel to access strategic and operational documents, but doing so is now "certainly more difficult," the former official said.

articles.title: Ukrainian helicopter gets new AI-assisted gun module against Shaheds
articles.body:
- The Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation delivered a Khyzhak combat module for aviation use, funded through a joint project with Uklon.
- The module fires a stabilized 7.62 mm PKT machine gun and uses AI-assisted tracking to help engage drones, including Shahed-type strike drones.
The Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation says it has delivered a remotely operated “Khyzhak” combat module for use in Ukrainian aviation, and that the system is now being used against Russian targets.
The foundation announced the delivery on social media, saying it purchased the module through a joint project with the ride-hailing company Uklon called “Pidsvity Voroha 2.0” (“Light Up the Enemy 2.0”). Video accompanying the post shows the module mounted on a helicopter and used against Russian Shahed-type strike drones.
“We are complicating flights for Russian Shaheds,” the foundation wrote. “The video shows the remotely controlled Khyzhak combat module, which the Foundation delivered for aviation. We purchased it as part of a joint project with Uklon, ‘Pidsvity Voroha 2.0.’ And now this module is successfully working against enemy targets, thank you for that!”
The Khyzhak module is built around a 7.62 mm PKT machine gun and can rotate 360 degrees horizontally and elevate up to 75 degrees vertically. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense codified the module and cleared it for use in the Armed Forces. The ministry said the machine guns mounted on the module can be loaded with either Soviet-pattern or NATO-standard 7.62 mm ammunition and that the platform is stabilized, allowing accurate fire while the vehicle carrying it is moving.
The module’s developers designed it to be modular. It can be installed on robotic ground platforms, mounted stationary, adapted for use on vehicles, or fitted to naval systems. The version shown in the foundation’s video represents an adaptation for aviation.
The module includes an artificial intelligence system for automatic target recognition and tracking, including automatic detection of drones. That capability allows operators to use the Khyzhak to engage small first-person-view drones as well as larger Shahed-type drones, which are roughly the size of a small Cessna aircraft, at close range.
The foundation did not disclose how many Khyzhak modules it has funded, which unit or units are operating the system, or the cost of the purchase made through the Uklon partnership.

articles.title: US and Iran Trade Strikes as Fighting Resumes in Gulf
articles.body:
U.S. Central Command launched a wave of strikes against Iran on Sept. 1, and President Donald Trump said forces are “prepared to do another one” as Iran launched retaliatory attacks Sept. 2.
Fighting resumed Aug. 30, as CENTCOM officials announced strikes on “minelaying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz.” Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has been using land-based launchers to lob floating mines into the Strait.
Speaking in the Oval Office on Sept. 2, Trump said he ended the roughly monthlong pause in hostilities because of sea mines.
“They were trying to rebuild their radar systems and a missile system and … to build a rocket that drops mines,” Trump said at a White House event. “They were building it, it was almost finished, so we took it out. We saw that they were building it, we see everything that they’re doing.”
Iranian forces countered with ballistic missile attacks on U.S. forces in Jordan and on civilian ships transiting the Strait. A number of U.S. Air Force personnel and assets are stationed at the base in Jordan that has previously come under attack.
On Sept. 1, CENTCOM announced additional strikes on IRGC targets in retaliation for “attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region.” The command indicated its targets included “air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine-laying capabilities, and communications sites.”
Trump called the U.S. strikes “a very heavy attack” that “took out all of the new equipment that they tried to build along the Strait of Hormuz: some defensive, some offensive.”
Iranian state media outlets alleged the strikes also hit a wedding party in a coastal town, but those claims remain unconfirmed.
Iranian forces launched their latest retaliatory strikes Sept. 2. Officials and media outlets in the Middle East reported attempted strikes in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, and Iraq. Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry also said Iran targeted a Saudi tanker in the Strait of Hormuz and killed members of its crew.
As of 4 p.m. Eastern time and 11 p.m. in much of the Middle East, CENTCOM had not announced additional strikes. Trump told reporters that the U.S. is “prepared to do another one anytime we want.”
CENTCOM continues to enforce a blockade of Iranian ships and ports and said in a Sept. 2 social media post that it has redirected 86 commercial vessels, disabled three, and boarded two as part of the blockade.

articles.title: Trump congratulates Hegseth on ‘good job’ after deadly Iran wedding strike
articles.body:
Trump congratulates Hegseth on ‘good job’ after deadly Iran wedding strike
US President Donald Trump has congratulated Secretary of War Pete Hegseth over the latest American strikes on Iran, despite one of the attacks hitting a wedding and killing several civilians.
Iranian authorities said two women and two children aged four and 16 were killed when a US munition hit a home hosting a wedding in Kuhestak, Hormozgan Province, on Tuesday. At least 67 others were wounded, many of them women and children.
According to weapons experts cited by AP and the New York Times, the fragments recovered at the site belonged to an American air-delivered guided munition, most likely a JSOW.
The Iranian Red Crescent has since asked the International Criminal Court to investigate the Kuhestak strike, while Iran’s UN envoy has urged the Security Council to condemn it.
US Central Command has said it is looking into the reports while insisting that American forces do not target civilians.
“You did a good job last night in Iran, by the way. You knocked the hell out of them,” Trump told Hegseth during an event at the White House on Wednesday. “We’re winning that one very big, by the way, in case you haven’t noticed,” he added, claiming that much of Iran’s naval and air capability has been destroyed.
Tehran responded to the latest wave of attacks by launching its own ballistic missiles and drones at US military facilities in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, and the UAE, as well as Erbil in Kurdistan Region, Iraq.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) later claimed to have killed “a number of enemy elements” and destroyed several drones in a missile and UAV attack on Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem Air Base.
Kuwait acknowledged that its air defenses had intercepted incoming missiles and drones but reported no casualties. Jordan said ten of 13 ballistic missiles that entered its airspace were intercepted.
Tuesday’s wedding strike follows several other incidents in which US attacks have caused heavy civilian casualties in Iran. On the opening day of the war in February, a US strike hit an elementary school in Minab, killing 175 people, most of them children. On the same day, a US strike also killed at least 21 civilians, including seven children, in the southern Iranian city of Lamerd.
Tehran has accused Washington of war crimes throughout the conflict, reporting up to 3,000 civilian casualties since the US and Israel launched their campaign against the Islamic Republic in February.

articles.title: How Israel kidnapped a senior Hamas security official in Gaza
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How Israeli forces kidnapped a senior Hamas security official from Gaza City
Israeli forces kidnapped a senior Hamas security official from his home in western Gaza City on Tuesday during an armed operation that killed his wife and wounded his son, according to Palestinian and Israeli sources.
Moen al-Arabid, head of Hamas' internal security apparatus in the Gaza Strip, was kidnapped after an Israeli special forces unit entered the area near the Katiba in western Gaza City, according to a Hamas source who spoke to The New Arab on condition of anonymity.
The source said the Israeli force, dressed in civilian clothes and travelling in two vehicles, including a white bus, entered the densely populated area before being discovered and engaging in an exchange of fire with Palestinian fighters.
Israeli drones subsequently carried out several strikes around the area, the source said, adding that the airstrikes provided cover for the Israeli forces during the operation.
According to the source, al-Arabid and his wife, Samah al-Khalidi-al-Arabid, confronted the Israeli soldiers inside their home.
Samah was killed during the confrontation, while their son, Obaida, was wounded, the source said, who added Obaida had been scheduled to celebrate his engagement on Wednesday.
The Israeli forces later arrested al-Arabid and removed him from the area while he was wounded, according to the source.
The source described the operation as a kidnapping rather than an attempt to kill al-Arabid, saying the Israeli forces had entered the area specifically to capture him alive.
One video appeared to show al-Arabid crawling along the ground while attempting to find cover. An Israeli bus then approached, and several projectiles were thrown in his direction.
The Hamas source said the projectiles were sound grenades rather than offensive grenades and were intended to distract the wounded man and prevent him from taking cover, facilitating his capture.
Israeli media later published a photograph purportedly showing al-Arabid after his arrest, depicting a handcuffed man who appeared to be injured.
Meanwhile, Palestinian sources also said that a vehicle attempting to leave the area toward eastern Gaza City came under attack about 200 meters from the site of the operation, causing additional casualties, including children.
Videos and photographs circulated on social media showed damage around al-Arabid's home, including a white bus with damaged windows and what appeared to be bullet marks.
Israel confirms arrest
Israeli officials confirmed that al-Arabid had been abducted during an operation in Gaza City.
Israeli Defence Minister Yisrael Katz said in a televised statement that Israeli forces were continuing their operations in Gaza City and had recently arrested a senior Hamas official.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed that al-Arabid was one of the "most prominent Hamas leaders in Gaza."
Netanyahu accused al-Arabid of helping hide and transport Israeli captives, attempting to rebuild Hamas' capabilities, participating in efforts to restore Hamas' rule over the Gaza Strip and spreading what Israel claimed was misinformation concerning the disarmament of Gaza.
"My directives are clear," Netanyahu claimed, saying that Israel would continue pursuing Hamas leaders and those involved in the 7 October 2023 attack.
Israeli Channel 12 reported that al-Arabid was wounded during the operation and transferred to Israel for medical treatment.
The Israeli Broadcasting Corporation, Kan, also quoted a security official as saying, "The target was wounded during the operation in the Gaza Strip and transferred to Israel for medical treatment."
According to Israel's Channel 11, the operation was planned and approved in recent days by Netanyahu and Katz. Kan reported that the Shin Bet security agency managed the operation.
Israeli sources cited by the channel said the operation was intended not only to obtain intelligence but also to send a message to senior Hamas leaders that they remained subject to Israeli pursuit despite the ceasefire.
Casualties in residential area
The operation caused casualties and damage in the surrounding neighbourhood in Gaza, which includes shelters for displaced Palestinians and is located near an American field hospital and a kindergarten.
Zaher al-Wahidi, director of the Information Centre at Gaza's Health Ministry, told TNA that ambulance and civil defence crews recovered four bodies and treated eight wounded people following the Israeli operation.
He said two children and two women were among those killed, including Samah al-Arabid, al-Arabid's wife.
The dead and wounded were transferred to al-Shifa Medical Complex, he added.
For residents living near the site, however, the operation was experienced not only through its casualties but through the sudden fear it caused among families, particularly those with children nearby.
Marwa Ezzat, a resident of the area, said her children were inside a nearby kindergarten when the clashes began.
She told TNA that the sudden gunfire and airstrikes sent residents into panic as families rushed to reach their children and move away from the area.
"We were terrified because our children were inside the kindergarten and we could hear the gunfire and explosions around us," Marwa said. "Everyone was trying to find a way to reach their children and get them to safety."
"After the operation subsided, displaced families gradually returned to their shelters and homes," she added. "Some found their tents and belongings damaged by shrapnel, while many children remained frightened by the possibility of renewed gunfire or airstrikes."
Intelligence and security objectives
Gaza-based Palestinian political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim told TNA that the operation appeared to have several objectives, including demonstrating Israel's ability to reach senior Hamas figures inside Gaza.
"Israel could have targeted al-Arabid from the air if its objective had been to kill him but instead chose to send a ground force to capture him alive," he said.
He added that the decision could indicate that Israeli security agencies wanted to obtain information from al-Arabid while he was alive, given his senior position within Hamas' security apparatus.
"The operation sends a message that the ceasefire does not prevent Israel from carrying out security operations inside Gaza," Ibrahim noted.
He explained that the arrest of a senior security official could give Israel access to sensitive information and create additional security risks for Hamas.
Hamas condemned the operation as a "serious crime" and accused Israel of deliberately endangering civilian lives.
The movement called on mediators and the U.S. administration to pressure Israel to stop what it described as violations of the ceasefire agreement.
In a press statement, Hamas said it had contacted mediators and Nikolay Mladenov, the UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, requesting "maximum pressure" on the Israeli government to halt its operations and implement the ceasefire agreement.
The operation came amid continuing tensions over the implementation of the ceasefire, with Israel and Hamas accusing each other of violations.
According to Gaza's Health Ministry, 1,326 Palestinians have been killed and 4,398 wounded in the Gaza Strip since an alleged ceasefire agreement took effect on 10 October 2025.
The ministry said the cumulative Palestinian death toll since the outbreak of Israel's genocidal war in October 2023 had reached 73,462, with 174,509 people wounded.
The kidnapping of al-Arabid adds another point of tension to the fragile ceasefire, as Israel says it will continue pursuing Hamas figures while the Palestinian movement and mediators seek to preserve the agreement and advance its implementation.

articles.title: Poland sent Ukraine 350 tanks—Europe just agreed to refund it half a billion dollars
articles.body:
Poland will recover hundreds of millions of euros from a shared European Union fund for weapons it handed to Ukraine, the defense outlet Militarnyi reported. The money had been frozen for two years and only started moving after a change of government in Hungary lifted a veto.
Europe's ability to keep weapons moving to Ukraine rests on members trusting they will be paid back for what they give away. When that cost-sharing seizes up, national governments face the full bill alone, and the case for the next donation gets harder. A single member's veto can jam that machinery for years.
The money starts flowing again
Poland will receive up to $500 million in 2027 from the European Peace Facility (EPF), an EU fund that reimburses member states for military aid to Ukraine. Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski told the Polish news agency PAP that the ceiling combines the $465 million now secured with a possible $12–35 million more, depending on which of the two payout options the European Commission picks. Warsaw had already collected $960 million earlier, bringing its total EU reimbursement to roughly $1.4 billion.
190 or 580 Patriot missiles? What Ukraine’s EU-loan request could buy—and why Washington still decides
The reimbursements had stalled in 2024, when Hungary blocked a $7.7 billion tranche. Budapest dropped the veto in June 2026 after a new government took over, unfreezing the funds. The bloc is now steering part of the money toward joint arms purchases and its training mission for Ukraine, rather than just reimbursement.
Where Poland stands among donors
By Militarnyi's tally of Kiel Institute figures, total Polish aid has reached $6.8 billion, with $5.2 billion of that military. That ranks Poland 11th among donors by raw volume. When weighed against each country's economy, it ranks 9th, equal to 1.021% of Polish GDP, with the military share at 0.775%.
A masked figure got into a Polish drone-parts plant—Poland now suspects a foreign spy service set the fire
What Warsaw handed over
Poland has supplied ammunition and other weapons since early 2022, before the full-scale invasion, and has since handed over more than 350 tanks—14 Leopard 2A4, about 60 PT-91 Twardy, and roughly 280 Soviet-era T-72 variants. Warsaw also sent Krab self-propelled howitzers, Piorun shoulder-fired air-defense missiles, and Grad rocket launchers. Alongside Slovakia, it was among the first NATO states to send Ukraine fighter jets, delivering 14 MiG-29 jets and 10 Mi-24 attack helicopters between 2022 and 2024.

articles.title: Lebanon receives first detainee of five to be freed by Israel
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Lebanon receives first detainee of five to be freed by Israel
Lebanon said it received a man on Thursday, freed as Israel announced it would release five people seized from the country's south, where it has fought several wars against Hezbollah in recent years.
The announcement came after Lebanon said its army received a man returned by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the first since Beirut called in August talks for the release of an initial group seized since the start of the 2024 war.
A source in the ICRC told The New Arab: "A humanitarian operation is currently underway, and to ensure the safety of everyone involved, we will not issue any further statements until after the operation is over".
"It was decided to release five Lebanese civilians who were arrested in areas under (Israeli army) control in southern Lebanon," the office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a statement.
"After their interrogation was completed, it became clear that they are civilians who are not members of any terrorist organisation, have not engaged in terrorism, and there is no reason to continue holding them in Israel."
The Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) said the man, identified as Malik Ghazi, was currently undergoing medical examinations, noting he was not registered on the Lebanese Association of Prisoners' list of missing persons.
A source in the association confirmed to The New Arab that they were not aware he had been captured.
"We usually inform residents about the capture or disappearance of a person and follow up on the matter and document it, but this did not happen with Ghazi. We learned today of the kidnapping of three people from the town of Helta in the south by Israel, and we are trying to find out the fate of these people," the source explained.
A source in the Lebanese Army told The New Arab that more prisoners are set to be handed over in the coming hours, but no specific times or dates were given.
Lebanese authorities have not officially announced the number of citizens Israel seized during that war and the ongoing hostilities, but a list of more than 30 people has been compiled by their families and a committee working on their cases.
The list includes at least one Syrian national and several Hezbollah fighters.
Netanyahu's office said the decision followed "extensive efforts" by Israel and Lebanon to locate and return the bodies of leaders of Lebanon's Jewish community abducted and killed in the 1980s during the country's 15-year civil war.
After the latest round of Lebanon-Israel talks in Rome last month, a Lebanese official said Israel gave Beirut a list of individuals to demand the return of their remains.
The Israeli military said in August it recovered the remains of a soldier killed in eastern Lebanon in 1982.
'Humanitarian operation'
Lebanon's state-run National News Agency said that the Lebanese army received Ghazi earlier on Thursday, adding that he was taken to an army intelligence headquarters in the southern city of Tyre.
Ghazi's family, from the southeastern town of Ain Ata, said in October last year that they had lost contact with him after he had gone out to exercise.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam hailed the release in a statement, thanking "the American administration... for the efforts exerted in this regard".
He pledged to work "until the release of all our prisoners" and "the disclosure of the fate of the missing", as well as an Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory.
Israel and Hezbollah have been engaged in hostilities since October 2023, when Tel Aviv launched the war on Gaza. What started as tit-for-tat attacks continued for a year before escalating into a full-blown war in 2024.
Hezbollah also drew Lebanon into the Middle East war two years later in support of its backer Iran after launching rockets at Israel, following joint US-Israel strikes on Tehran.
Israel responded with airstrikes and a ground invasion that Lebanon says have killed more than 4,300 people.
The conflict has calmed since a US-Iran memorandum of understanding and a framework agreement between Israel and Lebanon agreed in June.
The Lebanon-Israel deal calls for the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from south Lebanon and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in "pilot zones".
A date has not yet been set for the next round of Lebanon-Israel talks, and Israel still carries out strikes on Lebanon while occupying parts of its territory.

Leaked Documents Reveal Covert Russian Missile Technology Transfer to Iran
Russia has been secretly helping Iran develop advanced supersonic cruise missiles through a multiyear covert technology transfer program, according to an investigation by the Financial Times, posted on September 1.
Codenamed “C430L,” the program began in 2023 and has continued into 2026.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
This advanced technology transfer is part of a broader military exchange between the two nations. It was previously reported that Russia is simultaneously using the landlocked Caspian Sea to ship explosives, ammunition, and drone components directly to Tehran, bypassing Western navies to help replenish Iranian military stocks following strikes by the US and Israel.
According to leaked Russian correspondence, travel records, and military patents obtained by the Financial Times, the initiative focuses on helping Tehran develop a ramjet propulsion system—a specialized engine that enables cruise missiles to sustain flight at several times the speed of sound.
Missile experts told the publication the technology is designed for anti-ship and land-attack cruise missiles capable of threatening naval vessels and missile defense systems in the Middle East.
The program was arranged by Russia’s state arms exporter, Rosoboronexport, in coordination with defense contractor NPO Mashinostroyenia. Financial Times noted that senior Russian missile designers and propulsion specialists made repeated trips to Iran to assist with the project.
According to the Financial Times, NPO Mashinostroyenia engineers received technical data from an Iranian flight test and provided detailed technical analysis to help troubleshoot combustion, fuel system, and airflow issues in the Iranian prototype.
While Iran has previously flight-tested ramjet components, mastering supersonic air-breathing propulsion has remained a key technological hurdle for its defense industry.
The Financial Times reported that correspondence between Russian and Iranian officials regarding the next development phase of C430L continued through mid-2026.
Russia’s export revenues have also temporarily surged by 27% year-over-year in the second quarter to $125.7 billion, driven by global energy price spikes and Middle East supply disruptions. Driven by climbing Urals crude prices and expanded agricultural quotas, the brief foreign currency influx strengthened the ruble through late May.

articles.title: Ukrainian Drones Strike Russia’s $60 Million Kasta-2E2 Radar in Zaporizhzhia

Ukrainian Drones Strike Russia’s $60 Million Kasta-2E2 Radar in Zaporizhzhia
Ukrainian drones struck a Russian Kasta-2E2 radar station in the Zaporizhzhia region, with the hit confirmed through objective monitoring, Ukraine’s General Staff reported.
According to the General Staff, the strike took place on September 1 near the settlement of Vyshneve in the Zaporizhzhia region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian drones struck both the radar’s antenna and the equipment station of the vehicle operating the Russian system. The General Staff did not provide further details on the extent of the damage.
The Kasta-2E2, also designated 39N6, is a Russian mobile three-coordinate radar system designed to detect and track aerial targets flying at low and extremely low altitudes. The system determines the coordinates of detected targets and transmits the data to air defense command posts.
The radar is capable of detecting aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles, including targets operating at very low altitudes. Its detection range extends from approximately 5 to 150 kilometers (3 to 93 miles), while its altitude coverage reaches up to 6 kilometers (3.7 miles).
A small drone flying at an altitude of around 60 meters can reportedly be detected by the Kasta-2E2 from a distance of approximately 30 to 44 kilometers (19 to 27 miles), depending on the height of the radar’s antenna mast, which can be raised to as high as 50 meters.
Depending on its configuration, the estimated cost of a Kasta-2E2 radar system starts at approximately $60 million.
Ukraine’s General Staff reported that Ukrainian forces targeted multiple Russian military sites in the occupied Donetsk region and Russia’s Bryansk region on September 1 and overnight into September 2. The military also confirmed that earlier operations had destroyed a Russian MiG-29 fighter jet and a Ka-27 helicopter.

articles.title: Badenoch says UK must prepare for possible war by 2030
articles.body:
Kemi Badenoch has said Britain must increase defence spending to 3 per cent of GDP by 2030, warning that the country could face a major conflict within the next four years and arguing that higher military spending can no longer be delayed.
In a speech on Britain’s defence on Thursday, the Conservative leader linked the spending requirement to Russia, cyber attacks, threats to critical infrastructure and wider instability, while setting out the case for the £10 billion annual increase in defence spending announced by her party.
Badenoch said: “Before the summer, Keir Starmer was given intelligence that Russia could launch an attack on NATO as soon as 2030. Not enough politicians in Parliament have fully appreciated what that means. By that of course I mean Labour politicians. What this means that within the next 4 years, the UK could be at war with the world’s biggest nuclear armed state. Because under Article 5, an attack on any NATO country is an attack on all of them.”
She also referred to Russian naval activity around Britain and threats to undersea infrastructure, saying: “Vladimir Putin has called Britain Russia’s number one enemy. Russian warships have been sailing through the English Channel and the undersea cables which power our internet and power our entire information and communication network have come under threat. People may not see it in their day to day lives, but hostile states are constantly pushing the boundaries with unconventional warfare.”
Badenoch argued that national security needed to encompass more than conventional military forces, pointing to cyber security, energy infrastructure and national resilience.
She said: “National security is not just about tanks, boots on the ground and planes in the air. It is about our cyber defences, it is about our energy security, it is about our country’s resilience. National security does not just happen we also have to pay for it, and that means spending more money on defence.”
The Conservative leader compared the UK’s position with increased defence investment elsewhere in NATO, citing Poland’s expansion of its armed forces and higher German defence spending. She also referred to Greece already spending around 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence.
Badenoch said: “Being an island might make us feel safer, but it does not prevent conflict from coming to us. And let’s be honest, conflict is coming. We must act now. Because the defence of the nation is the first duty of government.”
She called for defence spending to rise every year until reaching 3 per cent of GDP by 2030, saying: “We need to increase our defence spending every year so we can get to 3% of GDP by 2030, anything after that is too late.”
The Conservatives have proposed increasing annual defence expenditure by around £10 billion by 2029/30 compared with current government plans. The party says the increase would be funded through welfare reductions and reallocating money from other areas of government expenditure, including civil research and development, the British Business Bank and the National Wealth Fund.
Badenoch said: “Finding the money to pay for defence means making tough choices, it means making difficult trade-offs.”
She added: “We have now completed our work to get to 3%.
“And today my team have set out our plan to remove the housing benefit and remove the VAT exemption for Motability, alongside savings from the disastrous Chagos Deal,
“And repurposing money from the British Business Bank into defence, we will be able to hit that 3% target.
“And let’s be clear, 3% is the minimum our country needs to stay safe.”
The speech also connected defence policy with the wider state of the economy, with Badenoch arguing that Britain’s ability to sustain greater military expenditure depends on controlling borrowing and public spending.
She said: “Defence is not separate from the economy. Fiscal responsibility is part of national security.”
Badenoch also repeated the Conservative proposal for a £17 billion Sovereign Defence Fund, which the party says would support military readiness and investment in the British defence industrial base.
The Labour Party was approached for comment on Badenoch’s remarks and the Conservatives’ defence spending proposals, but had not responded at the time of publication.
Closing the defence section of her speech, Badenoch said: “Russia will attack a country it thinks is weak. It will not attack a country it knows is strong.
“We need to be strong. If you want peace, you prepare for war.”

articles.title: Britain wants laser armed ground vehicle drones
articles.body:
Britain is seeking counter-drone technology that could lead to autonomous laser weapons mounted on Army vehicles and, later, uncrewed ground vehicles, with £5 million available immediately through a new Ministry of Defence competition, the department has said.
Project PANOPTES, launched by UK Defence Innovation on behalf of the MOD, is intended to develop an integrated Counter-Uncrewed Aerial System force-protection capability able to deal with massed and low-cost aerial threats without rapidly exhausting conventional ammunition stocks.
The MOD stated: “Defence seeks additional capacity to detect, track, identify, decide and defeat mass and low-cost threats in a cost-effective manner and without being overwhelmed or exhausting stockpiles. This is particularly acute for deployed land forces, but the problem is applicable to the protection of defence fixed infrastructure in the homeland.”
Although the competition is open to a range of technologies, laser directed-energy weapons are specifically identified as an area of interest. The MOD said: “Based on research, the Authority is particularly interested in capabilities centred on Laser Directed Energy Weapon (LDEW) effectors but is open to submissions relating to credible alternative novel approaches.”
The intended configuration would place the counter-drone capability on a military ground platform. According to the procurement documents: “To address the challenge described above we are looking to deliver an integrated C-UAS force-protection capability capable of autonomous operation, mounted on an Army vehicle.”
The system is intended to protect deployed forces against complex and saturation attacks involving small uncrewed aircraft, including simultaneous threats designed to overwhelm local air defences or force troops to expend comparatively expensive missiles and ammunition.
The MOD stated: “The capability should protect deployed troops against complex and saturation attacks designed to overwhelm existing defences or deplete conventional munition stocks. It should deliver more affordable combat mass against emerging air threats than legacy systems, and should exploit open architectures, platform-generated power, modular design and capable of autonomous operation.”
The initial threat focus covers representative Class 1 UAS and other small aerial targets. These could include individual drones as well as repeated, sequential or simultaneous attacks used for surveillance, targeting, disruption or attempts to exhaust defensive systems.
A later objective would move the capability onto an unmanned ground platform. The MOD stated: “Integration of the capability onto a future uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) is a planned objective. The solution should provide a scalable pathway towards future Army and Joint Ground-Based Air Defence (GBAD) capabilities as well as considering possible export opportunities.”
UK Defence Innovation has confirmed that Project PANOPTES is open to UK-based innovators and that a share of £5 million is available immediately. Stage 1 will act as an initial screening process, with applicants outlining their proposed technology before successful teams are invited to develop more detailed proposals.
The first phase is not intended to produce a complete operational counter-drone system. The MOD said: “The scope of Phase 1 is to identify and support organisations to accelerate development of their existing technology towards a final deployable system. It is not intended for the Phase 1 competition to seek delivery of a complete operational C-UAS system.”
Successful technologies could then be matured through later phases into demonstrable Minimum Viable Products before selected systems are developed into Minimum Deployable Capabilities for an initial operational user group.
The notice states: “Capabilities that demonstrate operational benefit may subsequently be developed further for wider adoption as part of a future Programme of Record.”
The wider procurement has an indicative value of £125 million excluding VAT, rising to £150 million including VAT. That figure is not an approved programme budget. The MOD stated: “The stated figure in this notice of £150,000,000 inc. VAT is aligned to the current understanding of the Strategic Defence Review, but this does not mean that this funding has been approved and is an indicative figure only.”
Stage 1 submissions are due by midday on 23 September. A launch webinar will be held on 9 September to provide potential suppliers with further information on the operational requirement before the competition moves into its subsequent stages.

articles.title: Trump weighs declaring Iran war over as Pentagon extends Middle East deployments
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump is privately considering declaring the war with Iran over, even as the Pentagon quietly extends troop deployments in the Middle East, according to a Wall Street Journal report on Wednesday.
The newspaper reported that Trump has discussed with senior aides "whether to declare the Iran war over," a move the president reportedly "favours." He believes that maintaining intense economic pressure will eventually force Tehran to "either dismantle its nuclear programme or collapse."
The US launched Operation Economic Outcast last week, targeting Iran’s key economic lifelines, including its oil, shipping, aviation, gold, technology and digital asset sectors.
Despite the private discussions, the Pentagon is extending deployments in a sign that the war could drag "well into next year.”
The military is maintaining 50,000 troops and 19 warships, including two aircraft carriers and 13 guided-missile destroyers, to provide the president with operational "flexibility."

Ukraine’s Patriot Arsenal Gets Another Lifeline as Spain Pledges More Missiles
Spain will continue supplying Ukraine with missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said on September 3, reinforcing Madrid’s commitment to one of Kyiv’s most urgently needed defenses against Russian ballistic missile strikes, according to euDebates.tv on September 3.
Ukraine has repeatedly urged its partners in recent months to increase deliveries of Patriot interceptors as Russian forces continue using ballistic missiles in large-scale strikes against cities and critical infrastructure.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Asked whether Spain would continue providing the missiles, Albares gave a direct answer.
“We have been doing this for a long time, and we will continue to do so,” the Spanish foreign minister said during an informal meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.
The commitment is particularly significant because Patriot remains one of Ukraine’s most important systems for intercepting ballistic missiles, while stocks of the specialized interceptors required for those engagements remain limited.
Albares had met Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha a day earlier, on September 2, on the sidelines of the EU foreign ministers’ gathering in Wicklow.
Their discussions focused on continued assistance to Ukraine, protection of civilians and the defense of critical infrastructure.
During the meeting, Albares reaffirmed Madrid’s support for Ukraine and its intention to increase missile deliveries.
Previously, Spain transferred five Patriot PAC-2 interceptor missiles to Ukraine from an air defense artillery regiment based at a Marine Corps facility in Valencia.
After that, reports emerged that NATO and European Union countries were urging Spain and Greece to provide Ukraine with Patriot interceptor missiles, focusing on PAC-2 stocks that are approaching the end of their shelf life.
The requests were made over the summer as Ukraine faces growing demand for air defense interceptors amid intensified Russian missile strikes. One option under discussion would see Norway purchase the missiles from Spain and Greece before transferring them to Ukraine.
