articles.title: Republican Senator Calls On Trump to Replace Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
articles.body:
Republican Sen. Thom Tillis is urging President Donald Trump to replace Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth because of what he described as “inept management.”
The North Carolina lawmaker’s call to oust Hegseth comes after Dan Driscoll resigned from his role as Army Secretary on Monday, amid tension that had been reportedly broiling between Driscoll and Hegseth for months. In a social media post on Wednesday, Tillis thanked Driscoll “for his leadership to our Army and service to our country,” before going on to slam Hegseth.
“If we had a @SecWar who maintained the same priorities and forward-thinking, he would be fighting to retain talented leaders like Dan and the many flag officers he has forced into retirement,” Tillis said. “Instead, he is creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks.”
Tillis, who previously served on the Senate Armed Services Committee, included in his post a link to a CBS News article that lists about 20 military and civilian leaders who have been ousted or stepped down since Hegseth was confirmed to lead the Department of Defense, including Driscoll. Also among them is Gen. Randy George, who was serving as the Army Chief of Staff until Hegseth requested that he retire, effective immediately, in the spring.
Tillis voted to confirm Hegseth as Defense Secretary last year, though he initially had reservations about him. Amid mounting controversy surrounding Hegseth’s nomination, three other Republicans broke from party ranks and voted against it, forcing Vice President J.D. Vance to be the tiebreaking vote. It was the smallest margin for the confirmation of a nominee to lead the Defense Department since the Secretary role was first formed in 1947, Senate records indicate.
Despite Tillis’ crucial vote in the confirmation, he has since publicly criticized the Defense Secretary. The Republican Senator told POLITICO in May that he thought that “Hegseth misinformed [the President] on the challenges” related to a war in Iran, adding that “I’m glad the president did what he did in Iran. I’m not glad that he has Hegseth advising him on the details.” He went on to tell the news outlet: “I’d love to see Pete Hegseth fired because he’s incompetent and doing a horrible job. That’s kind of on a Christmas wish list.”
And he renewed those calls on Wednesday.
“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis said in his post on X. He accused Hegseth of being “intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force.”
“I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it,” Tillis continued.
Tillis and Trump have clashed in the past, most notably when the North Carolina Senator joined two other Republicans in the upper chamber in voting against the President’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” last year. In the aftermath, the President lashed out at Tillis, threatening to back candidates who could challenge Tillis in a Republican primary race.
Soon after, Tillis announced that he would not seek reelection in the 2026 midterms, citing what he described as a shift away from bipartisanship in Washington in recent years.
“Too many elected officials are motivated by pure raw politics who really don’t give a damn about the people they promised to represent on the campaign trail,” Tillis said in a statement last June. He added that a choice “between spending another six years navigating the political theatre and partisan gridlock in Washington or spending that time with” his family is “not a hard choice.”
Trump has remained firm in his support for Hegseth. Amid speculation that Hegseth is considering launching a 2028 presidential bid, a reporter asked the President if he would back the Defense Secretary in such an event.
“I think he’s doing a fantastic job, but it’s very early to talk about that,” Trump said. “We have to get through the midterms first, and I think he’s a very good guy.”
“Right now, all [Hegseth] loves is, and all he cares about is, the military and taking care of the military,” he continued.
Hegseth has denied that he is considering running for President in 2028.

articles.title: China wants to back Egypt's push into AI. The US isn't happy.
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
China wants to help Egypt build out a local AI industry. The US isn't happy.
Egypt has emerged as unlikely battleground in the global AI race as China and the US vie for influence in the North African country.
News that Chinese tech giant Huawei had offered to take the lead on developing the country's AI datacentres surfaced just days before President Xi Jinping landed in Cairo for his first state visit in more than a decade.
The company has proposed exporting 1,408 of its most advanced Ascend 950-series chips to train AI models and 600 others for two clusters to run AI models after they're trained, Bloomberg reported on 26 August. It submitted a plan to build the datacentres inside 12 months, according to documents seen by the business news outlet.
The offer marks the first challenge to American AI dominance in the Middle East and if it goes through would be first known incidence of Huawei chips being exported abroad.
US companies have so far focused their efforts on lucrative markets in the Gulf, where the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Bahrain have received billions of dollars of investment in large-scale datacentres, cloud infrastructure and AI research institutions.
But news of Huawei's offer appears to have caused concern in the Trump administration, which is reportedly trying to rally American tech firms to consider a rival bid. The State Department is thought to have reached out to Microsoft and chip designers Nvidia and AMD to explore options.
Egypt, a country under-resourced in money and energy for AI development, has until now not been on Washington's radar. That it should now be the focus of conversations in Washington underlines the importance the Trump administration places on preventing Chinese AI from making inroads abroad.
Huawei's bid also hints at the role Beijing sees for AI as it tries to compete with the US in the Middle East and elsewhere. It dovetails with Xi's message this week to Arab capitals reeling from the US-Israeli war on Iran: Reject external interference and build a new security architecture.
Huawei has a longstanding relationship with Egypt, where it has for years worked on advanced technology projects including 5G, battery storage and cloud computing.
But it also trails far behind its American rivals in terms of international reach in AI and semiconductors. US export controls have drastically limited its access to cutting-edge technology, and though it is developing indigenous capabilities of its own, it is yet to challenge properly challenge America's dominance. Sealing the deal with Egypt would lay down a marker that proves that Chinese companies can compete with the America's tech giants.
China is vying for influence in other ways. In July it launched the first international body focused on AI development - World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation – which attracted signatures from 30 countries, mostly in the developing world. Beijing says the goal of the body is to ensure the development of advanced AI systems is inclusive and safe.
WAICO has been compared in some quarters to the US-led Pax Silica, an international initiative launched by the Trump administration last year to decrease reliance on Chinese supply chains.

articles.title: West trying to draw India into ‘games’ against China – Lavrov

West trying to draw India into ‘games’ against China – Lavrov
Western countries are trying to draw India into a confrontation with China by pushing a more military role for the Quad grouping, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said at the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) in Vladivostok. 
Lavrov said India feels “very uncomfortable” in the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) grouping, arguing that the US and Japan have sought to add a military component to it. 
“They are conducting maritime security exercises and are keen to draw our Indian friends into games against another great friend of ours – the People’s Republic of China,” Lavrov said.
The Quad grouping of India, the US, Japan, and Australia focuses on cooperation in the Indo-Pacific. Its activities cover areas ranging from trade and critical technologies to maritime security, with the four countries also taking part in the annual Malabar naval exercise.
At a meeting hosted by India in May, Quad foreign ministers launched a maritime surveillance initiative aimed at increasing information sharing and maritime domain awareness. India is also due to host the grouping’s next Quad-at-Sea Ship Observer Mission, intended to improve interoperability and knowledge-sharing.
📹 Germany Wants To Be Europe’s Top Military Force ‘Again’... Lavrov Points To Nazi Past, Calls It ‘Extremely Dangerous’

Lavrov linked the grouping to what he described as a broader Western effort to weaken the central role of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) by creating smaller blocs in the region.

The four countries already cooperate in a separate defense format, sometimes referred to as the SQUAD. Their defense ministers agreed last year to deepen maritime and air activities and strengthen what they described as regional deterrence and response capabilities.

articles.title: US military operation against Iran could extend into 2027 — WSJ

NEW YORK, September 3. /TASS/. Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth is quietly extending the deployment of US troops in the Middle East, acknowledging the possibility that the operation against Iran may not end this year, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported, citing sources.

articles.title: External involvement fuelling Sudan war, new report finds
articles.body:
Outside forces fuel Sudan war, new report finds
Foreign recruitment and external support networks are fuelling the brutal conflict in Sudan, independent UN human rights investigators said on Thursday in a new report, calling for accountability as fighting continues between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
This action is strengthening the military capabilities of the warring parties and enabling increasingly sophisticated military operations with devastating consequences for civilians, according to the report by the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan.
The report documented the involvement of transnational entities operating in several countries in recruiting, training, and deploying foreign personnel to support the RSF, as well as facilitating the transfer of weapons, ammunition, and military technology, and providing logistical support.
It also concluded that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the SAF used foreign-supplied drones in operations that harmed civilians and civilian objects.
Civilians bearing the brunt
The mission pointed to the "strict international legal obligations" incumbent upon States linked to these supply chains, which require them to exercise due diligence, investigate and stop illicit mercenary and supply networks operating from or through their territories, prevent violations, and enforce the UN arms embargo.
“The consequences of this external support are being felt most acutely by civilians,” said Mohamad Chande Othman, Chair of the Fact-Finding Mission.
“This external support has not brought greater protection for civilians. Instead, civilians are paying the price through attacks on homes, hospitals, schools, markets and places of refuge.”
The mission said it had documented the deployment of up to 2,000 former Colombian military contractors who were directly involved in operating combat drones, artillery and advanced weapons alongside RSF units in Darfur and Kordofan.
The report concluded that there are reasonable grounds to believe that private entities, logistical facilitators, and recruiters operating from countries including Colombia and the United Arab Emirates used transit points in Chad, southeastern Libya, and the Somalian city of Bosaso to facilitate the delivery of personnel, training, weapons, and logistical supplies to the RSF in Sudan.
Drone capabilities expanded
Mona Rishmawi, an expert member of the mission, said it had identified “a transnational chain of networks spanning several countries” that provided the RSF with foreign personnel, training, weapons and logistics.
“This support fed into RSF operations in Zamzam camp and later during the takeover of El-Fasher, where the Mission documented grave human rights and international humanitarian law violations and international crimes, including conduct displaying hallmarks of genocide,” she said.
The report also found that foreign suppliers have substantially enhanced the drone capabilities of both the RSF and the SAF, enabling them to strike far beyond front lines.
Translate warnings into action
The investigators called on States to enforce the arms embargo on Darfur, halt military transfers where there is a substantial risk of contributing to serious violations, investigate individuals and entities involved in illicit support networks, and strengthen accountability measures.
They also urged the Security Council to extend the arms embargo to cover all of Sudan.
Mr. Osman recalled that the international community has received repeated warnings about the violations in Sudan.
“Those warnings must now translate into action,” he said.
"Protecting civilians in Sudan requires taking action not only against those waging this war, but also against the individuals, entities, and networks that enable its continuation."

articles.title: India, Sri Lanka, and Israel’s overlooked Indian Ocean opportunity  - opinion
articles.body:
While Sri Lanka is not an obvious priority in Israel’s Asian policy, with India, Japan, and Singapore receiving far more strategic attention, it has considerable potential because of its location, its development needs and the direction its relationship with India is heading.
During my recent visit, this became particularly clear. The island sits close to major sea lanes and within India’s immediate maritime security environment. For New Delhi, Sri Lanka is not simply another neighbor. Access to its ports and maritime infrastructure carries significance beyond bilateral relations.
Indian concerns about China’s research and survey vessels illustrate this sensitivity. The issue is not simply Chinese commercial investment. New Delhi is also attentive to the possibility that external actors could gain access to ports, infrastructure, or oceanographic information with potential dual-use applications close to India’s coastline.
Sri Lanka should not be reduced to another arena of India-China competition. Colombo has strong reasons to maintain relations with multiple partners, including China. Any Israeli strategy framed primarily around containing Beijing would misunderstand Sri Lanka’s interests and risk narrowing the space for cooperation.
India’s own approach has become broader. During Sri Lanka’s economic crisis in 2022, New Delhi provided some $4 billion in assistance. Since then, the relationship has moved beyond emergency support toward longer-term cooperation in energy, infrastructure, digital connectivity, trade, and security.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s April 2025 visit marked an important step. The two countries signed agreements on electricity interconnection, digital transformation and development, and, for the first time, a formal memorandum of understanding (MoU) on Defence Cooperation.
India, Sri Lanka and the United Arab Emirates also agreed to cooperate on developing Trincomalee as an energy hub.
The defense agreement did not create bilateral security cooperation: India and Sri Lanka already had substantial ties in training, naval visits, exercises, and capacity-building. Yet the MoU gave this relationship a more formal framework. Cooperation includes joint exercises, maritime surveillance, hydrography, capacity-building, and the provision of defense platforms and assets.
SLINEX is a regular bilateral naval exercise, and in April 2026 the two navies conducted their fourth bilateral diving exercise in Colombo, including complex underwater operations. Sri Lankan personnel have also participated in India’s wider IOS Sagar initiative.
Taken together, these developments suggest that India is progressively embedding Sri Lanka within a wider Indian-led maritime security architecture. This does not mean that Colombo is surrendering its strategic autonomy or that India is constructing a formal alliance system. India continues to prefer flexible partnerships. But New Delhi increasingly sees regional security as something built through training, maritime domain awareness, interoperability, capacity-building, and institutional cooperation.
For Israel, this creates an opportunity that deserves attention.
For years, Israel-India relations have been viewed primarily through defense cooperation, technology, and an expanding strategic convergence. Those ties remain important. But as India’s regional role grows, Israel should consider whether that partnership can also provide a basis for selective cooperation with third countries.
Sri Lanka offers a useful test case; there is evidence of Sri Lankan interest in expanding relations with Israel. In August 2026, Sri Lanka’s new ambassador to Israel identified agricultural technology, defense, and trade as areas in which Colombo would like to deepen cooperation.
Agriculture is an obvious starting point. India and Israel have spent years developing Centers of Excellence that combine Israeli agricultural technology with Indian institutions, local adaptation, and training. A similar trilateral initiative could bring together Israeli technology, Indian implementation experience, and Sri Lankan development priorities.
The potential goes further.
Maritime security is one area where Israeli capabilities could complement rather than compete with India’s regional role. Israel has relevant experience in sensors, electro-optics, unmanned systems, and maritime infrastructure protection. Cybersecurity and artificial intelligence are also important as ports, energy facilities, and digital systems become connected and vulnerable.
Israel’s comparative advantage lies not in establishing a military presence in Sri Lanka but in providing niche capabilities, technology, and practical solutions. India brings geographical proximity, political weight,and military-to-military engagement. Israel can contribute specialized expertise in maritime surveillance, cyber defense, AI, and critical-infrastructure protection.
This does not require a formal India-Israel-Sri Lanka strategic triangle. A more realistic model would be functional trilateralism: concrete projects addressing Sri Lankan needs. The India-UAE-Sri Lanka cooperation around Trincomalee provides a useful precedent, illustrating that third-country participation can complement Indian interests rather than challenge them.
Israel must also recognize Sri Lanka’s political sensitivities. Colombo has historically supported the Palestinian cause and continues to support a two-state solution. Treating Sri Lanka merely as another market for defense technology would therefore be politically shortsighted. A broader relationship combining agriculture, water, technology, trade, and carefully calibrated security cooperation would be more sustainable.
The larger lesson extends beyond Sri Lanka. As India becomes more influential across the Indian Ocean, Israel should think about India not only as a bilateral strategic partner but also as a platform for regional cooperation.
For decades, the focus has been on what India and Israel can do together. The next question is what their accumulated experience and complementary capabilities might allow them to do together elsewhere.
Sri Lanka may be one of the best places to begin.

articles.title: Norway seizes Russian Arctic science vessel at Kiev’s request
articles.body:
Norway seizes Russian Arctic science vessel at Kiev’s request
The Norwegian authorities have seized a Russian research vessel in Svalbard at the request of Ukraine’s state-owned energy company, Naftogaz, amid growing tensions between Moscow and NATO states over access to and control of the Arctic.
The Professor Molchanov was detained on Wednesday while docked in Barentsburg, a Russian settlement on the Norwegian-administered archipelago. The Governor of Svalbard said the move followed an August 31 order by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court granting Naftogaz the right to seize the ship. The vessel has been barred from leaving Barentsburg until further notice.
The crew and passengers aboard the vessel learned about the seizure from media reports, a TASS correspondent traveling with the expedition said. Russian Far East and Arctic Development Minister Aleksey Chekunkov said on Thursday that the crew is safe, adding that lawyers for the Arktikugol trust would soon issue a legal response and intended to challenge the seizure order.
The Professor Molchanov is a Russian state-owned research vessel operated by the country’s hydrometeorological service, Roshydromet. Alongside scientific expeditions, it has served since last year as a regular passenger and cargo link between Murmansk and Barentsburg, transporting scientists, employees of the state-owned Arktikugol, contractors, their families, and supplies to the Russian settlements on Svalbard.
Direct air links between Russia and Svalbard ceased in 2020, while direct maritime passenger service was restored in 2025. The Professor Molchanov is currently the only vessel operating the route, with ten round trips between Murmansk and Barentsburg planned for 2026.
Under the 1920 Svalbard Treaty, Norway exercises sovereignty over the archipelago, while signatory nations are granted equal rights to engage in commercial and scientific activities there. Russia has maintained a presence on Svalbard for decades, with Arktikugol serving as its principal economic operator on the islands.
Naftogaz said it sought the seizure as part of an international effort to enforce a Hague arbitration award over assets it lost in Crimea following the peninsula’s reunification with Russia in 2014.
Russia has rejected the arbitration tribunal’s jurisdiction over the dispute, arguing that the Crimean assets in question could not qualify as Ukrainian investments made on Russian territory under the relevant bilateral investment treaty.
Acting Naftogaz chief Sergey Fedorenko praised the move as “another important step toward restoring justice,” pledging to continue the hunt for Russian assets worldwide.
Naftogaz, which claims that Moscow currently owes it around $4.22 billion, plus interest and legal costs, has pursued Russian state property elsewhere in Europe. The Finnish authorities froze a number of Russian-owned properties in 2024 at the company’s request. The Kremlin vowed to challenge the measures, and the Russian Foreign Ministry denounced them as illegitimate and warned of possible retaliatory steps.
The latest seizure comes just weeks after Moscow issued unusually explicit warnings against Western attempts to detain Russian vessels.
President Vladimir Putin described plans to seize Russian ships and sell their property as “piracy and robbery,” warning that Moscow would respond in kind in any part of the world it considers appropriate. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Russia would choose its own targets, including vessels operating in the interests of countries that made these seizures their policy.
Tensions have been mounting in the Arctic. In an article published earlier this week, Lavrov accused NATO states of seeking to turn the region into a “new front” against Russia and its partners. He pointed to large-scale Western military exercises and expanding command infrastructure near Russia’s northern borders, warning that the buildup increased the risk of an armed confrontation with potentially disastrous consequences.
Lavrov maintained that Moscow wants the Arctic to remain an area of peace and cooperation, but warned that Russia would defend its interests “by all available means” if confronted with hostile actions.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Security service and defence intelligence deputy heads to be dismissed over standoff between employees

Zelenskyy: Deputy heads of Security Service and Defence Intelligence to be dismissed over standoff between employees
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has stated that the deputy heads of the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) and Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) are to be dismissed over an incident involving a shootout between employees of the two agencies.
Source: Zelenskyy's evening address
Quote: "Two individuals implicated in the shooting have been formally named as suspects – a Security Service officer and a Defence Intelligence officer. All the other circumstances of what happened are also being investigated, from the very first day of this entire situation."
Details: Zelenskyy said he had discussed the situation with Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko.
Zelenskyy said the actions of the heads of both agencies will be assessed based on the results of an internal investigation. Decisions regarding the deputy heads of the SSU and DIU have already been taken.
Quote: "Personnel decisions have already been made in both agencies – the deputy heads who bear responsibility for this situation will be dismissed. This is entirely fair – both agencies must be held accountable; both acted in a way that is absolutely unacceptable."
Background:
- On 1 September, the Russian Volunteer Corps The Russian Volunteer Corps is a military and political organisation established in 2022 that consists of Russian volunteers who have been fighting for Ukraine since 2014 said that its deputy commander for combat operations, Stepan Kaplunov, had been abducted by unknown individuals in the courtyard of the building where he was living.
- On the morning of 2 September, reports spread on social media about a shootout said to be between Defence Intelligence of Ukraine and the Security Service of Ukraine in Kyiv's Dniprovskyi district, and that it was somehow connected to Kaplunov's disappearance.
- Meanwhile, the SSU said in the morning that, together with DIU, it had foiled a terrorist attack against a leader of a Russian opposition political national movement who had arrived in Ukraine.
- Later, Kaplunov's lawyer, Taras Borovskyi, said that the serviceman had been released, but his whereabouts were unknown.
- On the morning of 3 September, the SSU released a video in which Kaplunov admitted to having links to Russia's Federal Security Service and said an attempt had been made to recruit him to assassinate Ukrainian military personnel and other individuals. However, his lawyer insists that the confession was made under duress.
- On 3 September, Kaplunov himself also stated that he had been abducted by SSU officers and described his time in a "secret prison", where he was threatened with "disappearing forever".
- Kaplunov also said that the SSU had attempted, with his help, to discredit Dmytro Ivanov, deputy commander of the Timur Special Unit, and Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the President's Office.
- Officers from the State Bureau of Investigation have opened a pre-trial investigation into the circumstances of the confrontation between SSU officers and DIU servicemen.

articles.title: Slovakia’s Fico ridicules Kiev’s demands for more money
articles.body:
Slovakia’s Fico ridicules Kiev’s demands for more money
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has ridiculed Ukraine’s continued demands for additional Western funding despite the EU already approving a €90 billion ($105 billion) loan for the country earlier this year.
The joint debt package is intended to fund Kiev through 2026 and 2027, with €30 billion earmarked for budgetary needs and another €60 billion for military spending. Nevertheless, Ukraine has continued to report major funding shortages. 
“Have you noticed that Ukraine is already crying that it has no money? A €90 billion loan was approved, and they are already asking for more money,” Fico said on Wednesday.
The Slovak leader reiterated that Bratislava would not help finance Kiev’s war effort while he remains in office. “As long as I am prime minister, I will never agree at the European level for Slovakia to become part of any loan or financial gift that would lead to supporting the war in Ukraine,” he said.
The loan, backed by joint EU borrowing, is structured on the assumption that it would be repaid if Kiev secures reparations from Russia, a prospect Moscow has dismissed as “unrealistic.” Slovakia, Hungary, and the Czech Republic have secured exemptions from the EU scheme.
Despite already receiving billions under the loan, Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky recently told European officials that his government still faces a roughly €23 billion shortfall and urged the EU to speed up payments.
Several EU countries have in turn revived calls to use more than €200 billion in frozen Russian sovereign assets to finance Ukraine. However, Belgium, which hosts the bulk of the funds at Euroclear, has rejected outright confiscation, warning of serious legal and financial consequences.
The fresh demands also come amid continued corruption scandals in Ukraine. The IMF recently acknowledged “slippage” in Kiev’s governance and anti-corruption reforms in July even as it approved another $690 million loan tranche.
One of the largest scandals has involved state nuclear company Energoatom, where Ukrainian investigators have uncovered a $100 million kickback scheme. Ukraine’s tax authorities also said this summer that more than 2,000 shell companies had been involved in suspicious foreign trade operations worth around $4.7 billion.
Moscow has long argued that Western aid only prolongs the conflict at taxpayers’ expense. Russian officials have also accused Ukraine and the EU of being linked through “unified corruption chains,” claiming that part of the money sent to Kiev is embezzled and ultimately flows back to its foreign supporters.

articles.title: Foreign support, drones fuel Sudan war and possible war crimes, UN probe says
articles.body:
Foreign weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks are helping sustain Sudan's conflict and expanding the warring parties' ability to strike deep into civilian areas, a United Nations fact-finding mission said in a report published on Thursday, warning that some attacks may amount to war crimes.
Sudan's war erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between Sudan's military and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) ahead of a planned transition to civilian rule. The conflict has devastated the country, displaced more than 14 million people and created what the United Nations has described as one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The UN mission said investigators found reasonable grounds to believe that a transnational network involving individuals and entities in the United Arab Emirates, Chad, Libya and Somalia supplied the RSF with weapons, military equipment, logistics, training and foreign personnel.
The UAE, Chad, Libya and Somalia, the RSF and Sudan's military did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters.
UAE, Chad deny allegations
The UAE rejected allegations that it had provided military, logistical, financial or political support to the RSF, and Chad said it remained neutral in the war and denied knowledge of weapons transfers through its territory, according to the report.
The UN mission also said it obtained evidence that Colombian contractors played a significant role in operating and maintaining drone systems and other advanced weapons used by the RSF. It estimated the total number of Colombian contractors involved could approach 2,000 and said some were present during operations around al-Fashir in Darfur.
Colombia told investigators it opposed mercenarism and was taking steps to address the participation of Colombian nationals in foreign conflicts.
Mass killings of non‑Arab communities when the RSF captured al‑Fashir bore hallmarks that point to genocide, the UN mission said in a previous report in February.
In the past, the RSF has denied such abuses, saying the accounts have been manufactured by its enemies and making counter-accusations against them.
The mission said its investigation into external support for Sudan's military was at an early stage but had found evidence that foreign-supplied combat drones and loitering munitions, which can hover over an area before striking a target, had expanded the army's long-range strike capabilities.
It said some of those weapons were used in attacks on civilian locations, including Yabus Market in Blue Nile State.
Drone warfare violated international human rights law, UN says
The report found both sides committed serious violations of international human rights law and international humanitarian law in their drone operations, with some conduct amounting to war crimes. Both sides have previously denied allegations of human rights abuses.
Expanded range, persistence and increasingly sophisticated capabilities enabled Sudan's military and the RSF to strike far beyond immediate front lines, and evidence points to both sides carrying out drone attacks that killed civilians and hit hospitals, schools, markets and displacement sites.
More than 1,000 civilians were killed in drone strikes between January and May 2026, according to figures cited by the report.
Between May and July 2026, repeated RSF drone attacks damaged electricity and fuel facilities in the North Kordofan capital of El Obeid, which was under SAF control as RSF pressure intensified in June this year. Strikes disrupted water supplies, healthcare, transport and other basic services in a city already under severe strain and partial siege, the mission said.
Among the cases highlighted in the report were SAF strikes on Ad-Da'ein Teaching Hospital in East Darfur that investigators said killed at least 70 people and left the facility non-functional.
The mission reiterated calls for enforcement of the Darfur arms embargo and urged the UN Security Council to extend it across all of Sudan.

articles.title: UK seeks vehicle-mounted laser defence against drone swarms
articles.body:
The Ministry of Defence has opened a competition for new counter-drone technologies intended to protect deployed troops from mass and low-cost aerial threats, with particular interest in laser directed-energy weapons and a requirement for an eventual system capable of autonomous operation from an Army vehicle, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The tender notice published on 2 September begins an iterative procurement process through the Commercial X Dynamic Market. The wider procurement carries an indicative value of £125 million excluding VAT, or £150 million including VAT, although the MOD makes clear that this funding has not yet been approved and later stages will depend on future funding decisions.
Setting out the operational requirement, the MOD stated: “Defence seeks additional capacity to detect, track, identify, decide and defeat mass and low-cost threats in a cost-effective manner and without being overwhelmed or exhausting stockpiles. This is particularly acute for deployed land forces, but the problem is applicable to the protection of defence fixed infrastructure in the homeland.”
On existing counter-UAS approaches, the notice states: “Current approaches are constrained by limited magazine depth, high cost-per-engagement, limited manoeuvrability, workforce intensity and the difficulty of adapting capabilities at pace as UAS threats evolve.” The MOD added: “Based on research, the Authority is particularly interested in capabilities centred on Laser Directed Energy Weapon (LDEW) effectors but is open to submissions relating to credible alternative novel approaches.”
The first phase will focus on technologies which already exist and could be accelerated towards a deployable system rather than procuring a finished counter-UAS capability immediately. The MOD stated: “The scope of Phase 1 is to identify and support organisations to accelerate development of their existing technology towards a final deployable system. It is not intended for the Phase 1 competition to seek delivery of a complete operational C-UAS system.”
For later phases, the department said: “Over later Phases, the Authority’s intent, aligned with their Integrated Procurement Model, is to identify and rapidly mature promising technologies as demonstrable Minimum Viable Products (MVPs). The Authority may then, at its discretion (and the criteria detailed below) select projects to be iteratively developed, integrated and proven as Minimum Deployable Capabilities (MDCs) for an initial operational user group.”
The notice continues: “Capabilities that demonstrate operational benefit may subsequently be developed further for wider adoption as part of a future Programme of Record. Suppliers will be notified of the criteria, selection processes, and competition format as these Phases arise.”
The intended configuration is also set out in the requirement. The MOD stated: “To address the challenge described above we are looking to deliver an integrated C-UAS force-protection capability capable of autonomous operation, mounted on an Army vehicle.”
On the attacks the system is expected to counter, the department said: “The capability should protect deployed troops against complex and saturation attacks designed to overwhelm existing defences or deplete conventional munition stocks. It should deliver more affordable combat mass against emerging air threats than legacy systems, and should exploit open architectures, platform-generated power, modular design and capable of autonomous operation.”
The initial threat focus is on representative Class 1 uncrewed aerial systems and related small aerial threats, covering single attacks as well as repeated, sequential and simultaneous profiles. The notice states that this includes threats intended to disrupt operations, conduct surveillance, target fixed or mobile assets, overwhelm local defences or force the disproportionate use of high-cost munitions.
The MOD also plans for the system to move beyond a crewed Army vehicle. It stated: “Integration of the capability onto a future uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) is a planned objective. The solution should provide a scalable pathway towards future Army and Joint Ground-Based Air Defence (GBAD) capabilities as well as considering possible export opportunities.”
Stage 1 will assess whether industry proposals can meet the problem statements, with suppliers required to submit an evidence-based high-level programme plan supported by demonstrations, modelling, analysis and testing where appropriate. The MOD states: “No contract shall be awarded at this stage, but success is required to continue to Stage 2. All suppliers who demonstrate achievement of the threshold criteria shall be invited to Stage 2.”
Stage 2 will require successful suppliers to develop their initial proposals into fully costed and contractable projects running for around six months. Contracts at this point will be awarded according to evaluation scores and available funding within a £5 million limit, with technical factors expected to account for between 60% and 80% of the assessment and commercial factors between 20% and 40%.
Stage 3 could involve either a further competition or negotiation of a single direct award depending on how many suppliers remain. The MOD says contracts at that stage will cover scaling and production alongside testing, assurance, safety and security, with break points where aspects of the system cannot be demonstrated within the required timescales.
The department states: “The stated figure in this notice of £150,000,000 inc. VAT is aligned to the current understanding of the Strategic Defence Review, but this does not mean that this funding has been approved and is an indicative figure only.” It adds: “The intention is to begin Stage 1 with immediate effect, but future stages will not proceed until funding has been allocated and approved.”
The MOD also warns suppliers that later funding is not guaranteed, stating: “There is no guarantee that future funding will be allocated or approved and the Authority may cancel the procurement process at any time. Bidders proceed knowing and accepting this risk that no effort shall be compensated.”

articles.title: Taiwan deploys Ching Tien I cruise missile
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Air Force has completed mass production and deployed its Ching Tien I long-range supersonic cruise missile, while an upgraded version is reportedly being developed with a range exceeding 2,000 kilometers.
The ministry's proposed 2027 budget includes a program for the Air Force to contract the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology to provide follow-on support for the weapon system through 2031, per Liberty Times. The funding covers routine maintenance and periodic inspections, indicating the system has moved into operational service.
Ching Tien I, formerly known as the Yun Feng missile, uses a ramjet engine and can reach speeds of up to Mach 3. It has an estimated range of 1,200 to 1,500 kilometers, potentially allowing it to strike military targets in central and eastern China.
Because of its large size and earlier design, the first-generation missile is deployed primarily from fixed underground positions and mountain shelters, Liberty Times reported. The military is now pursuing an upgraded version designed to address the vulnerability of fixed-site deployment.
Ching Tien II is reportedly being developed as a road-mobile system, with plans to mount the missile on a European-made 12-by-12 heavy truck chassis. The military is also evaluating the possibility of using railway tracks for deployment and launch.
The upgraded missile is expected to feature improved propulsion technology, including a scramjet engine and solid-fuel rocket propulsion, according to Liberty Times. Its top speed is expected to exceed Mach 5, while its range could increase to more than 2,000 kilometers.
Such performance could put targets including Beijing and Wuhan within the missile's range. The system is expected to become a major component of the nation’s asymmetric deterrence capabilities.

articles.title: 13 Yemen government forces killed in clashes with Houthis
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
13 Yemen government forces killed in clashes with Houthis
Thirteen Yemeni government forces were killed in clashes with Houthi fighters on Thursday, a military source told AFP, saying the group was trying to advance towards areas bordering the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait.
The Houthis launched a broad offensive along frontlines on the western Red Sea coast, in a bid "to advance toward Bab al-Mandab and areas held by government forces", he said.
"According to an initial toll, 13 government troops -- including two officers -- were killed," the source said, requesting anonymity.
The Bab al-Mandab strait is the chokepoint at the southern entrance to the Red Sea, a key maritime route for Saudi oil exports and other global trade.
Yemen, embroiled in more than a decade of civil conflict, in July became the latest country to be embroiled in the Middle East war as the Houthis upended a 2022 truce with Yemen's Saudi-backed government.
The rebels welcomed an Iranian plane to Yemen's capital Sanaa, setting off a spate of attacks. They later announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships and territory.
Another military source said most of those killed on Thursday were on the frontlines between the government-held coastal city of Mokha and the inland city of Taiz, while the others died in clashes near the Red Sea coast.
He said the Houthis were trying to sever the route connecting Taiz and Mokha to cut off the port city, which has come under relentless attack in the past month.
Official news agency Saba also reported "fierce fighting" between government forces and the Iran-backed group west of Taiz, as well as reporting Houthi missile and drone fire.
Saba reported "sustained escalation by the Houthi terrorist militia across several battlefronts west of Taiz and along the West Coast".
A field officer in Mokha told AFP his men were "fighting fiercely to repel the massive Houthi offensive".
"We also thwarted an attack with two booby-trapped boats that exploded near the port," he said.
Last month, Yemen's information minister Moammar al-Eryani warned that the Houthis were plotting to seize land along the Bab al-Mandab strait, which would allow them to further threaten the vital shipping artery.
The Houthis do not control the coastal areas bordering the strait, but they hold the key port city of Hodeida north of Mokha and have repeatedly attacked Saudi ships in the Red Sea.

articles.title: Japanese WWII crimes revisited: Soviet files detail mass beheadings in Manchuria
articles.body:
Japanese WWII crimes revisited: Soviet files detail mass beheadings in Manchuria
On August 9, 1945, a notorious Japanese army unit executed dozens of civilian prisoners in the city of Hailar, on the day the Soviet Union launched an offensive against the Imperial Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo.
To mark Victory over Japan Day (V-J Day), the Russian authorities published historical documents for the first time detailing the killings. The files were compiled by the Soviet military counterintelligence service (SMERSH), which investigated the crimes and brought some of those responsible to justice.
Hailar, then a city of around 40,000 people, now part of China’s Inner Mongolia region, saw some of the fiercest fighting of the Soviet-Japanese conflict, which began on August 9, 1945. A major Japanese fortified complex in the area, built with forced Chinese labor during the occupation, has since become part of a memorial park.
The crimes described in the documents released by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) took place elsewhere, at a secret police prison where the Japanese authorities held local residents suspected of harboring pro-Soviet sympathies.
Manchuria had a complicated history of Russian settlement. Its population included working-class railway builders, monarchists who had fled the Bolshevik Revolution, and even committed Russian fascists eager to ally themselves with the Axis powers.
How did the USSR go to war with Japan?
Despite fighting on opposing sides in World War II, the USSR and Japan avoided direct military confrontation through most of the deadliest conflict in human history. Soviet forces stopped a Japanese attempt to expand into Mongolia in 1939, but afterward, both powers concentrated on their principal enemies: Nazi Germany for Moscow and the United States for Tokyo.
The defeat of the Axis powers in Europe in May 1945 changed the strategic balance, while Moscow was also under pressure to honor a commitment to its Allied partners to enter the war in the Asia-Pacific.
Within weeks, battle-hardened Red Army forces overran Japan’s Kwantung Army in Manchuria and created a credible threat of an invasion of the Japanese home islands.
Japan ultimately chose to surrender to the Americans.
What was the Hailar massacre?
As the prospect of war with the USSR grew in 1944, the Japanese occupation authorities in Manchukuo compiled lists of Soviet citizens and other “subversives” and began arresting those deemed a threat. On August 9, another wave of arrests was followed by summary executions.
The organization tasked with the effort was the Tokumu Kikan, or Special Service Organizations, a network of elite military-civilian units specializing in human intelligence and fifth-column activities. The decentralized organization traced its origins to a force created in 1904 by Japanese intelligence officer Akashi Motojiro to conduct covert operations against the Russian Empire. It was reestablished in 1919 as Tokyo pursued plans for expansion on the Asian mainland.
Lt. Col. Amano Isamu, who headed the Tokumu Kikan branch in Hailar, ordered the killing of 43 people on August 9, 1945, with Japanese-commanded local police assisting in the operation.
Three weeks later, after the occupation regime collapsed, local residents exhumed the bodies so they could bury their relatives. SMERSH investigators established that many of those killed were Soviet citizens living in Hailar.
What evidence was found in Hailar?
The complete report assembled by Maj. Gen. Pyotr Popov, the SMERSH commander in Hailar, contained more than 100 pages of documents as well as a collection of photographs.
The FSB has declassified and published around 20% of the material, including excerpts from a medical examiner’s report, transcripts of interviews with witnesses and suspects, a description of the secret prison, and updates Popov sent to Moscow as the investigation proceeded.
Who were the victims?
According to the documents, Soviet forces learned about two mass graves exhumed by locals, while 19 bodies were still awaiting burial, allowing investigators to conduct proper post-mortem examinations. All of those killed were identified as ethnic Russians and Jews except for one Mongol man.
Messages left on the walls of prison cells provide a glimpse into the people held by the Tokumu Kikan. Many of the inscriptions simply contain victims’ names, including one reading ‘Gosha K’. Others include biographical details, dates of imprisonment, and complaints about torture, malnutrition, and deaths inside the prison.
A young man named Vinokhodov left a farewell message saying, “dying for the cause, I feel some relief,” suggesting that he sympathized with the Soviet Union.
How did the Japanese kill the prisoners?
The prisoners were killed by clean beheading carried out by a professional’s strong hand, the forensic report said. The evidence suggests that at least one of the executioners was an accomplished swordsman.
The documents state that several victims were not completely decapitated, with their heads left attached to their bodies by skin at the throat. Although Soviet investigators did not comment on this, it has significance in Japanese cultural tradition.
Traditional seppuku, a ceremonial form of self-disembowelment that also served as a form of capital punishment among the samurai class, was normally carried out with the assistance of a second person. The assistant would cut off the dying person’s head to end the suffering. A technically difficult cut that left the head partly attached was regarded as evidence of exceptional swordsmanship and was intended to preserve the dignity of the person being executed.
Seppuku was long outlawed by 1945, however, and it is highly unlikely that an Imperial Japanese officer intended to grant his prisoners an honorable death. A more plausible explanation is that the executioner was showing off.
One notorious episode during the Nanking massacre in 1937 involved two Japanese officers who were reported to have competed to see who could kill 100 people with a sword first. Contemporary Japanese newspapers portrayed the victims as battlefield combatants, although researchers have concluded that they were almost certainly prisoners of war.
What happened to the perpetrators?
In November 1945, a Soviet military tribunal sentenced Japanese military and police personnel involved in the mass arrests and executions in Hailar to death. Tokumu Kikan chief Amano and Maj. Gen. Haseki Kageyama, the head of the provincial gendarmerie, were among those executed by firing squad.
Their fate contrasted with that of many other Japanese officers, including Tokumu Kikan alumni, who were later incorporated into the US-backed postwar order. Former enemies, including individuals implicated in war crimes, offered their knowledge and experience to Washington as the Cold War began.
One example was Imperial Japanese spymaster Arisue Seizo. Gen. Charles Willoughby, who headed US military intelligence under Gen. Douglas MacArthur, recruited Arisue and similar figures to kickstart anti-Communist operations in Asia.
Why did Soviet citizens live in a hostile nation?
Russia became heavily involved in the development of Manchuria in the late 19th century as it sought greater access to Chinese markets. The Russian defeat in the Russo-Japanese War and the collapse of the Russian Empire during World War I, however, sharply reduced the country’s influence in the Far East.
Harbin, one of the main centers of Russian settlement in Manchuria, became a magnet both for people who wanted nothing to do with the new Soviet state and for those seeking to actively undermine it. Some younger Russian emigres in Manchuria came to believe that fascism could provide a path to restoring Russia, creating an organization that at its peak in the 1930s was estimated to have around 20,000 members.
The Russian community in Manchuria nevertheless remained sharply divided over the Soviet Union. According to historian Sergey Smirnov, around 120,000 people in the region in the 1920s were either Soviet citizens or sympathized with the new state, while more than 100,000 held opposing views.
The divide is also reflected in the newly released documents, which identify a “white emigree” surnamed Kaevich as a member of the Japanese police who took part in the Hailar massacre.
Where are the Hailar massacre archives?
The archives are held by three separate institutions.
The Central Archives of the Federal Security Service (CA FSB) holds interrogation transcripts, personal files and and background declarations of Japanese officers and medical personnel.
The Russian State Military Archive (RGVA) stores operational military records of the Soviet Red Army’s trans-Baikal offensive into Manchuria in August 1945.
The State Archive of the Russian Federation (GARF) stores the official state records, evidence compilations, and international legal paperwork regarding the 12 primary Japanese war criminals prosecuted by the Soviet Union for crimes against humanity in Northeast China.

articles.title: How Israeli settler violence is altering Palestinian geography
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How Israeli settler violence is altering Palestinian geography in the West Bank
Nablus, occupied West Bank - At Joseph’s Tomb in Nablus, Israeli military vehicles enter the city ahead of groups of Jewish settlers. Roads are closed within minutes. Movement in the surrounding neighbourhoods comes to a halt.
Palestinian residents retreat into their homes as tear gas drifts into nearby streets and buildings. The visits usually last only a few hours. But the military operation around them can disrupt daily life across the area, clearing streets and restricting movement to allow settlers to reach the site.
The scale of the deployment is striking: soldiers, armoured vehicles, road closures and movement restrictions are mobilised to facilitate a temporary settler presence in the heart of a Palestinian city.
That makes the visits more than religious pilgrimages. They are also demonstrations of who can move through Nablus, who is required to stay inside, and which authority can impose those restrictions.
Joseph’s Tomb is, however, a special case. Although it lies inside Nablus, in Area A, the Oslo Accords established particular arrangements governing access to the site. Military-backed visits therefore do not represent the sudden extension of Israeli control over the Palestinian Authority-controlled city.
But the exception is politically significant precisely because it exposes the gap between jurisdiction on paper and power on the ground. The Palestinian Authority remains formally responsible for Nablus, yet when a visit is authorised, Israel can deploy troops, close roads and secure a route for settlers. Israeli military power ultimately determines who can enter and who can move.
“Turning religious and heritage sites into instruments of political conflict is a dangerous development, as it conflates the sacred with the settlement project and transforms collective memory into a means of generating violence and forcibly reshaping the geography,” Dr Mona Abu Hamdiya, a researcher in heritage and archaeology, told The New Arab.
When an exception becomes the norm
The closures eventually end, but their effects are less easily erased.
Families plan around incursions. Work is disrupted. Relatives can be separated. Streets that are normally open become inaccessible. Residents learn that, for several hours, the ordinary rules governing their city can be suspended.
Repetition matters. An event that is officially exceptional can, through repeated incursions, become part of the landscape of Palestinian life.
Joseph’s Tomb therefore offers a lens through which to view a wider transformation underway across the occupied West Bank. The question is not simply whether Israeli sovereignty has formally changed, but whether the space available to Palestinians is being progressively narrowed while Israeli access, settlements and infrastructure become harder to reverse.
The figures suggest this is no longer a marginal phenomenon.
According to the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), more than 1,300 settler attacks resulting in Palestinian casualties or property damage were recorded across the West Bank in the first seven months of 2026, an average of more than six a day.
More than 2,300 Palestinians had been displaced by settler attacks and related access restrictions since the beginning of the year.
By late August, OCHA had recorded 23 Palestinians killed and more than 1,040 injured in settler attacks in 2026. Palestinians are now being injured directly by Israeli settlers at a rate of more than three a day, compared with two a day in 2025 and one every three days in 2020.
The pattern is particularly stark in communities close to settlement outposts, where attacks are accompanied by restrictions on access to agricultural land, roads, water and electricity.
Qusra, near Nablus, illustrates how these pressures can converge. In August, settlers established a new outpost in Area B near three Palestinian families in the Ras Al Ein area. OCHA reported increased settler and military presence, damage to water and electricity infrastructure and severe restrictions on the families’ movement. By late August, two of the four roads connecting the area to Qusra were under Israeli control.
The mayor of Sebastia municipality, Mohammad Abdul Aziz Azem, described the pressure on Palestinian communities as part of a broader effort to empty land of its Palestinian inhabitants and confine them to increasingly restricted population centres.
“This is being pursued through organised terrorism supported by Netanyahu’s government, amid international silence and the absence of effective deterrent sanctions against the Israeli occupation government,” he told The New Arab.
Violence changes the map
The significance of settler violence lies not only in the immediate harm it causes, but in what happens afterwards.
A farmer who is attacked must decide whether returning to a field is worth the risk. A family facing repeated threats may stop using a road. A community whose water infrastructure is damaged becomes more dependent on outside assistance.
When such violence is followed by little accountability, and Palestinians subsequently face restrictions on accessing land from which they have been driven, temporary intimidation can create a lasting change in who uses the territory.
Yesh Din, which has monitored Israeli police investigations into ideologically motivated offences against Palestinians since 2005, found that 93.6% of the cases it tracked ended without an indictment. Only 3% resulted in a conviction.
“Settler violence is part of a comprehensive strategy aimed at determining the outcome of the conflict through the silent annexation of Palestinian land,” Dr Hosam Al-Dajani, a writer and political analyst, told The New Arab.
“This is being pursued by forcibly displacing the population through a series of measures imposed by the occupation, including escalating violence and targeting trees, property, people, and everything that connects Palestinians to their land,” he added.
From coercion to administration
On the ground, the process can be incremental. An outpost appears on a ridge. Settlers begin using surrounding land. Palestinians face threats or attacks. Access roads are closed or restricted. Roads, electricity connections and other infrastructure follow, while military protection makes the new arrangement more secure.
Eventually, what began as an unauthorised presence can acquire some degree of official recognition or state support.
OCHA reported in August that at least 26 settlement outposts had been established in Area B over the previous two and a half years, 19 of them since the end of 2024. Peace Now estimates that settlers have taken control of more than 100,000 dunams in Areas A and B, including through violence and threats that have restricted Palestinian access to land.
The process is increasingly accompanied by administrative measures.
Israel’s land-registration programme, approved in February 2026, is intended to complete title-settlement procedures covering 15% of unregistered land in Area C over five years. Israel says the process will clarify ownership. Critics, including Peace Now, argue that formalising land rights while Palestinians face restrictions on access risks turning inequalities created under occupation into an administrative record.
The concern is not simply that a registry might transfer land illegally. It is that the conditions under which evidence of ownership is produced are themselves unequal.
A Palestinian family may have inheritance documents, tax receipts and generations of knowledge establishing its claim to a field. But if repeated attacks or access restrictions prevent the family from regularly cultivating it, absence can begin to look like abandonment.
An outpost, meanwhile, may acquire roads, electricity, security and eventually official recognition.
Coercion can therefore precede administration. Violence does not have to be formally ordered by the state to alter the conditions under which land is subsequently governed.
"Settler violence is part of a comprehensive strategy aimed at determining the outcome of the conflict through the silent annexation of Palestinian land,” Dr Hosam Al-Dajani, a writer and a political analyst, told The New Arab.
“This is being pursued by forcibly displacing the population through a series of measures imposed by the occupation, including escalating violence and targeting trees, property, people, and everything that connects Palestinians to their land,” he added.
“The objective is to impose new facts on the ground in order to advance this strategy, which violates international law and resolutions of international legitimacy, particularly UN Security Council Resolution 2334,” Al-Dajani said.
Annexation without a declaration
Calls to annex the occupied West Bank have grown louder since the far-right government came to power, with ministers openly stating their intentions to seize the Palestinian territory.
Yet at an official level, and to international interlocutors, Israel says that security measures protect Israelis, that registration settles ownership questions, and that borders should be decided through negotiations.
But any future negotiations would not take place over a fixed landscape. While the political status of the territory remains unresolved, the land Palestinians can reach, the authority they encounter and the evidence they can produce to establish ownership are already changing.
Since 2023, the UN says more than 6,200 Palestinians have been displaced by settler attacks and related access restrictions since 2023, including more than 2,300 in 2026 alone. Forty-six communities have been completely displaced.
The cumulative effect is territorial change without a formal declaration of annexation.
“Palestinians face a major challenge that requires unity and cooperation in confronting this project. The threat is not only to Palestinian land but also to the Palestinian national political project itself,” Akram Atallah, a political analyst and columnist for Al-Ayyam newspaper, told The New Arab.
“It is also undermining the two-state solution, as the territory on which a Palestinian state is supposed to be established is being fragmented and brought under increasing Israeli control.”
Mohammed Saleem is a Palestinian journalist, writer, and political analyst.

articles.title: Construction of British deep space radar to begin in 2027
articles.body:
Construction of the British site for the Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability will begin in April 2027 under a contract the United States Space Force signed with Northrop Grumman in August 2024, with planning permission sought in March this year and initial authority to operate already issued, according to a written answer published this week.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, was responding to Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative MP for Huntingdon, who had asked what progress had been made on establishing the capability, referring to paragraph 81 of the Defence Investment Plan.
Mr Pollard said: “The Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability (DARC) is a ground-based radar system that will provide 24/7, all-weather capabilities to detect, track, identify and characterise objects up to Geostationary Earth Orbit. DARC will require three permanent radar sites and a radar operations centre to provide 360-degree coverage: in Australia, the UK and the US. Construction of sites in Australia (Exmouth) and the US (IROC, Eglin) have been completed.”
He said: “The USSF signed a contract with Northrop Grumman on 23 August 2024 for construction of the UK site starting April 2027.”
On the regulatory position, he said the department has completed an environmental impact assessment including a landscape and visual impact assessment, to ensure the project has minimal impact on the local skyline, and that this formed part of a town planning application submitted to the local planning authority in March 2026.
He added: “The Defence Electromagnetic Authority, working with the Office of Communications, has issued an initial Authority to Operate. MOD and the Civil Aviation Authority is completing the necessary safety of flight procedures for local airspace.”
What DARC does
Most existing radars are optimised for low Earth orbit, where the majority of satellites and debris sit a few hundred kilometres up, and objects in geostationary orbit at around 36,000 kilometres have been tracked largely by optical telescopes, which depend on clear skies and darkness. A radar capable of reaching that altitude works regardless of weather or time of day, which is what the reference to 24/7 all-weather capability in the answer describes. The three sites, spread across Australia, Britain and the United States, provide continuous coverage of the geostationary belt as the Earth turns.
Geostationary orbit holds communications satellites, missile warning satellites and a substantial share of the space infrastructure military operations depend on, and both Russia and China have demonstrated satellites capable of manoeuvring close to others, which is a behaviour that cannot be characterised without being able to see it happening.
The United Kingdom site is at Cawdor Barracks in Pembrokeshire, west Wales, an existing defence site the Army had been due to vacate. The answer’s references to the local skyline and to safety of flight procedures for local airspace reflect the physical scale of the installation, which involves large parabolic dish antennas across a substantial footprint.
The programme is a trilateral effort under the AUKUS partnership, jointly funded by the three nations, with the American site at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida and the Australian site at Exmouth in Western Australia, which the answer confirms are both complete.
Britain’s wider space programme sits under UK Space Command, established at RAF High Wycombe in 2021, which brings together military space operations alongside the existing space domain awareness assets including the Fylingdales radar in North Yorkshire, itself part of the American ballistic missile early warning system.

articles.title: Russia Threw Six FPV Drones at Ukraine’s Armed Robot—It Completed the Mission Anyway
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Threw Six FPV Drones at Ukraine’s Armed Robot—It Completed the Mission Anyway
Ukraine’s Droid TW-12.7 unmanned ground vehicle survived five FPV drone strikes and completed its combat mission before a sixth hit finally disabled the platform, according to a DevDroid press release shared with UNITED24 Media on September 2.
Soldiers from the fire support company of Ukraine’s 74th Separate Reconnaissance Battalion deployed the UGV during a remotely conducted operation against a concentration of Russian troops.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
As the Droid TW-12.7 approached the position, two FPV drones struck the vehicle almost simultaneously. One of the hits damaged its aiming module, but the platform remained mobile and continued the mission.
Operators adapted to the damage by aiming in the direction of the weapon barrel and opened fire on the target. Two additional FPV drones struck the UGV during the engagement, but it remained operational long enough to complete its primary task.
The vehicle then began withdrawing and survived a fifth FPV strike while continuing to move. A sixth drone eventually disabled it on the return route.
DevDroid said the Russian troop concentration was cleared and enemy forces suffered losses. The entire operation was carried out remotely, allowing Ukrainian personnel to avoid direct contact with Russian troops.
“In this engagement, the enemy was able to stop the Droid only with the sixth FPV drone, but they still failed to prevent it from completing the mission. For us, this is what survivability means in practice: after being hit, a system must not simply remain mobile—it must retain enough functionality for its operators to complete the mission and achieve the intended result,” DevDroid CEO Yurii Poritskyi said.
The Droid TW-12.7 is a Ukrainian reconnaissance-and-strike UGV developed by DevDroid. It is equipped with a remotely operated turret carrying a 12.7 mm M2 Browning heavy machine gun, as well as an integrated ballistic computer and AI-assisted targeting functions.
The platform is designed to engage personnel, vehicles, and lightly armored targets while allowing Ukrainian troops to conduct dangerous frontline missions from a safer distance.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine is expanding its fleet of unmanned ground vehicles, aiming to produce at least 50,000 combat and logistics robots this year to reinforce infantry units and bridge manpower shortages along the frontline.
